entries.section: 1. The Lord magnifies Solomon

paragraphs.text: And Solomon the son of David was strengthened in his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him, and magnified him exceedingly. [1]

In the last chapter of First Chronicles it was said: “And the LORD magnified Solomon exceedingly in the sight of all Israel, and bestowed upon him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel” (1 Chr 29:25).

entries.section: 1. The Lord magnifies Solomon

paragraphs.text: The Lord says: “Them that honour me I will honour” (1 Sam 2:30). Solomon honored the Lord; he gave priority to the Lord. Before he sat on the throne to carry out any kingly work concerning the nation, he gathered all the leaders and the people and went to the high place at Gibeon to offer a sacrifice to the Lord at the tabernacle of God which Moses the servant of the Lord made in the wilderness [3].
He received a throne that was contested by his brothers, but the Lord strengthened and magnified him, because He was with him.

In this book Solomon appears in wealth, greatness, authority and glory from the beginning of his enthronement, without stressing his increase in these things as the Book of Kings does. For this book presents Solomon to us as a type of the Lord Christ, who came down to carry humanity to His heavens and to grant them fellowship in the glories. If in His humility He became poor, it was only to enrich us by His poverty; His glories are not outside Him, rather He is the source of riches, righteousness, holiness and glory, and He desires to give us Himself, so that we may see in Him all sufficiency.
v There is none good but one, that is, God, who alone also brings happiness to man, and gives him peace, stability and tranquility[1].

St. Basil the Great v In honoring God we honor ourselves. He who opens his eyes to look at the light of the sun receives joy in it... Those who honor God do this for their salvation and for their great benefit; how? Because he who follows virtue glorifies God... Let us glorify God and bear Him in our bodies and our spirits (1 Cor 6:20)[2].
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 2. The tent of meeting first

paragraphs.text: 2 Then Solomon spake unto all Israel, to the captains of thousands and of hundreds, and to the judges, and to every governor in all Israel, the chief of the fathers. 3 So Solomon, and all the congregation with him, went to the high place that was at Gibeon; for there was the tabernacle of the congregation of God, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness. 4 But the ark of God had David brought up from Kirjathjearim to the place which David had prepared for it: for he had pitched a tent for it at Jerusalem.
Then Solomon spake unto all Israel, to the captains of thousands and of hundreds, and to the judges, and to every governor in all Israel, the chief of the fathers [2]
It is clear that those around Solomon in positions of leadership were lovers of worship, so they shared with Solomon his love for communal devotional life.

entries.section: 2. The tent of meeting first

paragraphs.text: So Solomon, and all the congregation with him, went to the high place that was at Gibeon; for there was the tabernacle of the congregation of God, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness. [3]

Gibeon was at one time the greatest sanctuary in Israel; by then it had become merely a station on the road to Jerusalem. The defects that spoil the beauty of Gibeon as a center of worship are not mentioned (1 Kgs 3:3-4). There is the tent of meeting, the tent of God which Moses the servant of the Lord made in the wilderness... and the bronze altar which Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, made, and he put it before the tabernacle of the Lord (2 Chr 1:3-5).

All the children of Israel gathered around King Solomon, and it describes here his journey with all Israel to Gibeon. The book mentions here details that are not found in the Book of Kings [3-6], to state that what Solomon does comes as an extension of what Moses did of old. The king wanted to affirm his sanctification and esteem of the tent of meeting which Moses the prophet had set up about 300 years earlier, and of the bronze altar that Bezaleel made (Ex 31:2-4; 38:22-31). So the building of Solomon's temple does not mean the destruction of the worship that Israel inherited; rather it is an extension of it, bearing the same thought[3].

Solomon began his reign with a popular visit to the tent of meeting and the altar of the Lord. It was a good opening to his work, as everyone felt the need for God's presence in their midst, and for their own presence in the house of the Lord, and indeed for the Lord to be in their company throughout the journey of their life.

entries.section: 2. The tent of meeting first

paragraphs.text: But the ark of God had David brought up from Kirjathjearim to the place which David had prepared for it: for he had pitched a tent for it at Jerusalem. [4]

entries.section: 3. The altar and the sacrifices

paragraphs.text: 5 Moreover the brasen altar, that Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made, he put before the tabernacle of the LORD: and Solomon and the congregation sought unto it. 6 And Solomon went up thither to the brasen altar before the LORD, which was at the tabernacle of the congregation, and offered a thousand burnt offerings upon it.
Moreover the brasen altar, that Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made, he put before the tabernacle of the LORD:
and Solomon and the congregation sought unto it. [5]

The secret of the power of the tent is the altar, which points to the Cross and the sacrifice of the Lord Christ for the salvation of the world. Through the Cross we bear the righteousness of the Crucified, and so we become righteous in the eyes of God. With this we sing, saying: “For the eyes of the Lord are over the righteous, and his ears are open unto their prayers: but the face of the Lord is against them that do evil” (1 Pet 3:12).

The going of the leaders and the people with Solomon to Gibeon, where the tent of meeting and the altar were, signifies our accompanying the crucified Lord Christ, the King of Peace, that we may enjoy the heavenly dwelling and experience the Cross, the power of God unto salvation (Rom 1:16).

entries.section: 3. The altar and the sacrifices

paragraphs.text: And Solomon went up thither to the brasen altar before the LORD, which was at the tabernacle of the congregation, and offered a thousand burnt offerings upon it. [6]
Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on the altar [6], and perhaps more than that of peace offerings, a sign of joy and gladness before the Lord.

At the beginning of his account of Solomon, the writer stressed that he offered a thousand burnt offerings on the bronze altar, and when God appeared to Solomon He said to him: “I have chosen this place to myself for an house of sacrifice” (2 Chr 7:12). If the number 1000 in the Bible often points to heaven and the heavenly things, then this book, which concentrated on the temple and worship, aims to proclaim the opening of the gates of heaven to the Jews as well as to the Gentiles, so that the Church of the New Testament, which embraces everyone, may offer the sacrifice of the perfect burnt offering, that is, perfect love for God, just as Abraham offered his beloved son as an acceptable burnt offering and a pleasing aroma before God.

Some scholars observe that Chronicles does not mention the sin offering or the trespass offering, so that the altar appears as though it had been dedicated to burnt offerings and peace offerings. The building of the house of the Lord is a call addressed to all humanity to rise and share with the heavenly ones the sacrifices of praise, thanksgiving and glorification, as an expression of love and response to God's surpassing love for His rational creation.

While St. Ignatius was rejoicing in the Spirit on his way to martyrdom, he expressed his view of the Church as the surrendered Body of Christ; for Christ offers the Eucharist, His Body and Blood given up, so that the Church may live, enjoying with her crucified Bridegroom the spirit of self-giving. This is what led him to define the Church as the “place of sacrifice, Thysiasterion” in more than one place[4].

v May God increase you in riches; be gracious with these gifts to those who regard them and desire them, for I am a priest of my Lord Jesus Christ and to Him I offer the sacrifice every day, and I wish to offer my life as a sacrifice, as He offered His life as a sacrifice out of love for me[5].
Ignatius, bishop of Antioch

entries.section: 4. God appears to Solomon

paragraphs.text: 7 In that night did God appear unto Solomon, and said unto him, Ask what I shall give thee. 8 And Solomon said unto God, Thou hast shewed great mercy unto David my father, and hast made me to reign in his stead. 9 Now, O LORD God, let thy promise unto David my father be established: for thou hast made me king over a people like the dust of the earth in multitude.
In that night did God appear unto Solomon, and said unto him, Ask what I shall give thee. [7]

Since Solomon took care to speak with the leaders in a spirit of love, and set out with them to the tent of meeting, and offered a thousand burnt offerings on the altar, the Lord appeared to him, asking him about his needs.

Most likely the prophets Nathan and Gad were counselors to David the prophet and king, but it seems that there was no prophet in the days of Solomon, so the Lord Himself appeared to him and spoke with him. This does not mean that he was better than his father, with whom God spoke through His prophets, for God works by one means or another according to what the need requires. He spoke directly with some men of the Gentiles, such as Abimelech (Gen 20), and Pharaoh's Egyptian servants (Gen 40), and Pharaoh himself (Gen 41).

The word “ask” and its derivatives occur eight times in God's speech with Solomon here. For a man's request, especially from God, reveals to a great extent what is in his heart. If Solomon had been a warrior, he would have asked for victory over his enemies; but since he saw that he was a young leader who needed wisdom to manage the affairs of the people of God, and that he was the successor of the great king David, he therefore asked God for wisdom.
It is stated in Josephus, the Jewish historian, that when God appeared to Solomon, he leaped from his bed[6].
The Lord does not cease to ask us: “Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name: ask, and ye shall receive, that your joy may be full” (Jn 16:24).

v What you ask is counted as nothing compared with what I want to give you. For what did you ask in my name? That the demons be subject to you. Do not rejoice in this, for what you have asked is nothing; for if that were something, He would be asking them to rejoice...
[That your joy may be full], that is, ask for what satisfies you.
When you ask for temporal things you ask for nothing. “Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again” (Jn 4:13)...
Ask for what satisfies you!

Speak in the language of Philip: [Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us] (Jn 14:8). [The Lord said to him: I have been with you all this time, and you have not known me? He who has seen me, Philip, has seen the Father also] (Jn 14:9) Vulgate.
Offer thanks to Christ, who became weak for your sake because you are weak, and let your desires be prepared for the divinity of Christ, that you may be satisfied by them[7].

entries.section: 4. God appears to Solomon

paragraphs.text: v His saying “whatsoever ye have asked” must not be understood as any request whatever, but anything that truly bears on the blessed life. And what follows, “Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name” (Jn 16:24), is understood in two ways: either you have not asked in my name, since you did not yet know my name as you ought, or you have asked nothing, if it is compared with what you ought to ask, so that what you ask is counted as nothing[8].
St. Augustine

entries.section: 4. God appears to Solomon

paragraphs.text: And Solomon said unto God, Thou hast shewed great mercy unto David my father, and hast made me to reign in his stead. [8]

A sense of gratitude with thanksgiving: “hast made me to reign in his stead”; You have placed me in the place of my father, the pious, righteous and great man, who completed his mission in a spirit of sincerity. It is as though he says, with Elisha to his spiritual father Elijah: [He gives me two portions of your spirit](*). Would that we carried the same spirit, so that we feel that the divine blessings our fathers received are an asset for us, which it befits us to enjoy.
His father David had received mercy from God, for although he sinned, through repentance he enjoyed the mercies of God.

entries.section: 4. God appears to Solomon

paragraphs.text: v “No one is clean from defilement, even if his life is one day”[9]. David groans, saying: [In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother bore me] (Ps 51:5). The Apostle also declares: “For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Rom 3:23-25). Therefore forgiveness of sins is granted to those who believe, since the Lord Himself said: “For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins” (Mt 26:28)[10].

entries.section: 4. God appears to Solomon

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great v Although the servants of God and His friends avoid the sins that are unto death, and practice many good works, we do not believe that they are without trivial sins, for God does not lie when He says: [No child whose life is one day on the earth is without sin](**). Add to this the blessed John the Evangelist, who without doubt is no less than Job in worthiness, and who declares: [If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us] (1 Jn 1:8). Moreover, we read in another place: “For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again” (Prov 24:16)[11].

entries.section: 4. God appears to Solomon

paragraphs.text: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles v You quoted the following statement from the Book of Job: [No one is clean, even if his age on earth is one day] (Job 4:14-5) LXX. And you added: “for we are guilty after the likeness of Adam's transgression[12]”, an opinion that your book on the prophecy of Jonah declares in an honorable and clear way, where you affirm that the little children of Nineveh were justly obliged to fast with the people merely because of their ancestral sins[13]. Therefore it is not improper for me to put the question to you: Where did the soul commit the iniquity from which it is obliged, even at this age, to be delivered by the mystery of Christian grace?[14]

entries.section: 4. God appears to Solomon

paragraphs.text: v No man is without sin, whether his life is one day or he has lived many years. If even the stars are not pure in the sight of God(***), how much more the worm and the corruption into which those who were subjected to the sin of Adam's disobedience have fallen?[15]
St. Augustine

entries.section: 4. God appears to Solomon

paragraphs.text: Now, O LORD God, let thy promise unto David my father be established: for thou hast made me king over a people like the dust of the earth in multitude. [9]

“Let thy promise be established”: the best thing we ask of God is that He fulfill in us His divine promises to our fathers and to us, and to all humanity. “Remember the word unto thy servant, upon which thou hast caused me to hope” (Ps 119:49).

entries.section: 5. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge

paragraphs.text: Give me now wisdom and knowledge, that I may go out and come in before this people: for who can judge this thy people, that is so great? [10]

It is not mentioned here that he was a young lad who did not know how to go out or come in (1 Kgs 3:5-15), because he is a type of the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God. Rather it is said that he needed wisdom to go out and come in before the people and to judge them.
Solomon, as a true son of his father David, chose spiritual blessings, not temporal ones. Solomon knew that these gifts please God, and that He is the Giver of them (Prov 2:6).

“For who can judge this thy people, that is so great?” A beautiful sense of the weight and gravity of responsibility, together with confidence and certainty in God's possibilities and His gifts to us.
Solomon did not ask for wisdom in order to boast of it, but to serve the people of his Lord in a spirit of godliness, and to judge among them in a spirit of justice.

entries.section: 5. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom says: [Since Solomon asked what ought to be asked, see how quickly he received. Two things must be in the one who prays: that he asks with zeal, and asks what ought to be asked[16].]
v David slept a peaceful death as though he were sleeping, and in his place came the boy Solomon to reign.
He (the Lord) said to him: [Keep my commandments as your father did, arise and rule over the kingdom of David your father.
Then I will be with you, and I will magnify your name in the world. If you are with me, you keep my commandments and do my will](****).
The boy knelt to pray before God, a pure prayer full of beauty to whoever contemplates it.
The virgin boy offered a pure prayer to the Lord, with words of love, and the Lord heard it in His exalted place.
O God of my father David, accept my prayer, and do not depart from me, for You have chosen me to become king.
Give me a heart full of the mysteries of hidden things, that I may judge Your people with faithfulness and righteousness (1 Kgs 3:7-9).
I am a boy, so be to me a chief teacher, wiser than any scribe, and guide the son of David, direct him and teach him, and give him wisdom.
I did not ask You for abundance of riches, but that I may know how to govern according to Your will (1 Kgs 3:9-11).

entries.section: 5. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge

paragraphs.text: I did not ask, nor will I ask, for the souls of my enemies, but I ask only for a heart full of the mysteries of faith (1 Kgs 3:11)[17].
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh

entries.section: 6. God gives more than we ask

paragraphs.text: 11 And God said to Solomon, Because this was in thine heart, and thou hast not asked riches, wealth, or honour, nor the life of thine enemies, neither yet hast asked long life; but hast asked wisdom and knowledge for thyself, that thou mayest judge my people, over whom I have made thee king: 12 Wisdom and knowledge is granted unto thee; and I will give thee riches, and wealth, and honour, such as none of the kings have had that have been before thee, neither shall there any after thee have the like.
And God said to Solomon:

Because this was in thine heart, and thou hast not asked riches, wealth, or honour, nor the life of thine enemies, neither yet hast asked long life; but hast asked wisdom and knowledge for thyself, that thou mayest judge my people, over whom I have made thee king [11]

Where did this idea come from? If we return to (1 Chr 22:11-12), we hear the voice of David the prophet saying to his son: “Now, my son, the LORD be with thee; and prosper thou, and build the house of the LORD thy God, as he hath said of thee. Only the LORD give thee wisdom and understanding, and give thee charge concerning Israel, that thou mayest keep the law of the LORD thy God.” Solomon was listening to the voice of his father. Therefore, when the Lord asked him: “Ask what I shall give thee?” he immediately said: [I desire wisdom and knowledge] [11].

entries.section: 6. God gives more than we ask

paragraphs.text: Wisdom and knowledge is granted unto thee; and I will give thee riches, and wealth, and honour, such as none of the kings have had that have been before thee, neither shall there any after thee have the like. [12]

God gave him riches, wealth and honor, although he did not ask for these things. Those who renounce the things of the world, the Lord gives them to them in abundance. The Lord Christ says: “Seek ye... the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you” (Mt 6:33).

He asked for himself wisdom or discernment, that is, he asked for practical wisdom through which he lives the life that befits a believer. God gave him intellectual and practical wisdom, so that there was none like Solomon until the Lord Christ came, who is greater than he (Mt 12:42; Lk 11:31). The Lord of glory Jesus promised us that if we seek the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, He will give us the other things, because they will not possess us or distract us from the Giver, nor corrupt our hearts (Mt 6:33). Together with heavenly grace He gives us our temporal needs, since all earthly goods become for our good; but without grace these goods enslave our souls.
v Then the Lord spoke with him, and said to him: I have chosen you, and I will not forsake helping you.

And because your mouth asked for righteous judgment (1 Kgs 3:13), and you hated wealth and empty glory, I will give you riches and glory with greatness, and your fame will spread everywhere and in the countries (1 Kgs 3:3).
And they will come on journeys, and see how great your wisdom is, and the report of you will spread among the kings and peoples of the earth, and every quarter will obey your fear[18].
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh

entries.section: 7. Solomon, his chariots and his horses

paragraphs.text: 13 Then Solomon came from his journey to the high place that was at Gibeon to Jerusalem, from before the tabernacle of the congregation, and reigned over Israel. 14 And Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen: and he had a thousand and four hundred chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen, which he placed in the chariot cities, and with the king at Jerusalem. 15 And the king made silver and gold at Jerusalem as plenteous as stones, and cedar trees made he as the sycomore trees that are in the vale for abundance. 16 And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt, and linen yarn: the king's merchants received the linen yarn at a price. 17 And they fetched up, and brought forth out of Egypt a chariot for six hundred shekels of silver, and an horse for an hundred and fifty: and so brought they out horses for all the kings of the Hittites, and for the kings of Syria, by their means.
Then Solomon came from his journey to the high place that was at Gibeon to Jerusalem, from before the tabernacle of the congregation, and reigned over Israel. [13]

entries.section: 7. Solomon, his chariots and his horses

paragraphs.text: And Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen: and he had a thousand and four hundred chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen, which he placed in the chariot cities, and with the king at Jerusalem. [14]
The king was forbidden to multiply horses (Deut 17:16), lest he imitate the pagan kings who think that their greatness and glory lie in outward displays.
Solomon thrust himself into a forbidden arena, for his good father did not ride in a chariot, nor mount a horse; the most he mounted was a mule.

entries.section: 7. Solomon, his chariots and his horses

paragraphs.text: And the king made silver and gold at Jerusalem as plenteous as stones, and cedar trees made he as the sycomore trees that are in the vale for abundance. [15]

The book affirms that God fulfilled what He promised Solomon, giving him, together with wisdom, riches and glory. Solomon made gold and silver like stones, and cedar trees like the sycamore; the abundance of gold, silver and precious wood makes them cheap and lowers their value, whereas the abundance of grace increases its value.

entries.section: 7. Solomon, his chariots and his horses

paragraphs.text: And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt,
and the king's merchants received the jalība at a price [16]
(See the commentary on 1 Kgs 10:28).
Jalība: some think that it means yarn or linen threads, for which Egypt was famous.

entries.section: 7. Solomon, his chariots and his horses

paragraphs.text: And they fetched up, and brought forth out of Egypt a chariot for six hundred shekels of silver, and an horse for an hundred and fifty: and so brought they out horses for all the kings of the Hittites, and for the kings of Syria, by their means. [17]

Solomon opened trade relations with Egypt, so he imported horses and linen, which he manufactured and exported to Syria at great profit (1 Kgs 10:28-29). Perhaps he learned that from his mother, who was like one of the virtuous women: “She makes garments and sells them, and delivers girdles to the Canaanite” (Prov 31:24).
Now everything was settled, and the situation was ready to begin the building of the temple.
In Your company I walk the royal road
v You were with Solomon, so he walked the royal road.
He was strengthened and learned much, because he clung to You.
With divine wisdom he did not work alone, but clung to all the leaders, not to show off his abilities, his knowledge and his wisdom,
but to set out with them to the tent of meeting.
And under Your shelter he enjoyed Your divine presence.
v Strengthen me, O my God, that I may walk the royal road.
I work with You, and in the shadow of Your grace.
I work with my brethren, and I do not separate myself from them!
In the midst of my brethren I meet You, O Lover of mankind!
v Would that You appear before me as You appeared to Solomon.
That I may hear Your divine voice, and so possess You!
In You and through You I enjoy divine wisdom.
You are the secret of my riches, my satisfaction and my joy.
You are the secret of my success and my happiness!
I hold fast to Your divine promises, as my fathers held fast to them.
v I walk in the royal road, and do not turn from it to the right or to the left.
I feel no want or need.
The silver of the world and its gold become like stones.
And the chariots of the world and all its possessions are as nothing.
v You lift my heart up to Your heavens.
And my soul is carried away as in a heavenly chariot.
I rest in You, and I am established forever.
The currents of the world do not terrify me.
And the trials of life do not break me.
I pass through all my life a joyful journey in Your company!
My soul is at peace, and the doors of my heart, my mind and my emotions open to You!
By Your cross You opened to me the gates of Paradise; by Your grace You open the gates of my inner man!
Enter, O King of kings, into my depths, and let Your Kingdom be established within me!

entries.section: 1. The inner preparation for the building

paragraphs.text: 1 And Solomon determined to build an house for the name of the LORD, and an house for his kingdom. 2 And Solomon told out threescore and ten thousand men to bear burdens, and fourscore thousand to hew in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred to oversee them.
Solomon presents to us a method of building, whether spiritual or temporal, which is to begin with the inside before a person asks about his needs from outside.
And Solomon determined to build an house for the name of the LORD, and an house for his kingdom. [1]

Solomon issued his order to build a house for the name of the Lord, and also to build the royal palace. It is noticeable in this order that he proclaims the priority of the house of the Lord, and at the same time does not ignore the needs of the state, that is, building a palace to manage the affairs of the state. Spiritual work does not mean laxity or neglect or ignoring temporal obligations and responsibilities. Moreover, he did not ask for a house for his personal comfort and to display his greatness, but asked for a house for his kingdom, that is, to serve the state, to receive his subjects, and to be an honor to the state among the other states. It is as though the first house is for the glory of God, and the second for the common good. He does not seek what is for himself, but rather what is for the Lord and for his brethren.

The original Hebrew text says: “and a royal house for him”, used for administering the kingdom and as a palace for his dwelling. This palace required high-level planning; the planning and building took about thirteen years (1 Kgs 7:1-12).

Solomon inherited from his father the longings of his heart, and fulfilled what David used to dream of, as he sang, saying: “One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple” (Ps 27:4).

[I will not enter the tabernacle of my house, nor go up into my bed, I will not give slumber to mine eyes, nor sleep to mine eyelids, until I find out a place for the LORD, an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob] (Ps 132:3-5).

In the wilderness the people used to bring offerings and sacrifices to the movable tabernacle, and now that they had settled in the Promised Land, and the prophet David had made huge efforts to expand the kingdom, the time had come for the house of the Lord to be built, especially since David had prepared much material and many designs, and had made the leaders and the people ready for the work.

entries.section: 1. The inner preparation for the building

paragraphs.text: And Solomon told out threescore and ten thousand men to bear burdens, and fourscore thousand to hew in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred to oversee them. [2]

Some see that the personality of Solomon differs from that of his father David: David was the simple shepherd who loved the people of God and served them with all his heart, while Solomon was the man famous for the wisdom given to him by God to set up buildings, especially the temple of God.

David was the military commander who was occupied with battles from his youth on behalf of the people of God, relying on God, the Giver of victory. Solomon, however, was the man of politics, who tried to win the nations around him, that they might support him in carrying out his projects.

David was the ideal leader, who did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, so that he was counted the standard by which every king of Judah was evaluated; Solomon, on the other hand, was ideal in his wisdom, and his credit is that he built the temple (Jn 10:23; Acts 3:11; 5:12), which the Jews to this day long to rebuild.

Some see that Solomon thought he had elevated his people, as he brought them into the family of the nations, and entered into commercial treaties that brought prosperity and glory to his people in his days. But the cost was heavy and bitter after his death and for long generations, for his policy caused his people to decline spiritually.

entries.section: 2. He asks the king of Tyre for a skilled man

paragraphs.text: 3 And Solomon sent to Huram the king of Tyre, saying, As thou didst deal with David my father, and didst send him cedars to build him an house to dwell therein, 4 Behold, I build an house to the name of the LORD my God, to dedicate it to him, and to burn before him sweet incense, and for the continual shewbread, and for the burnt offerings morning and evening, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts of the LORD our God. This is an ordinance for ever to Israel. 5 And the house which I build is great: for great is our God above all gods. 6 But who is able to build him an house, seeing the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain him? who am I then, that I should build him an house, save only to burn sacrifice before him? 7 Send me now therefore a man cunning to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass, and in iron, and in purple, and crimson, and blue, and that can skill to grave with the cunning men that are with me in Judah and in Jerusalem, whom David my father did provide.
And Solomon sent to Huram the king of Tyre, saying,
As thou didst deal with David my father, and didst send him cedars to build him an house to dwell therein [3]
After Solomon had numbered the men working in his state, he turned to the king of Tyre in a spiritual, gentle and wise manner.

Solomon sent to Huram, perhaps to thank him for his congratulations on his enthronement as king, and at the same time to ask for his help in building a temple for the Lord. Here we note the following:

a. He begins his message by revealing the good relations that existed between Huram, king of Tyre, and his father David, as though his own relationship went back to an old and genuine friendship without a blemish [3]. David had spoken with Hiram about building the house of the Lord and about the covenant with God (1 Kgs 7). So Solomon asked the king of Tyre for a sign of the development of a genuine friendship marked by affection.

b. He is not setting up a memorial monument for his father, but building a temple for God, whom the heavens and the earth cannot contain. What occupied Solomon was neither his own temporal glory nor the glory of his father, but the glory of the living God.
c. With some clarity Solomon reveals to Huram his purpose in building the house of the Lord his God, namely that the people, with their priests, may practice the following:

entries.section: 2. He asks the king of Tyre for a skilled man

paragraphs.text: · To dedicate it to Him [4], that is, to bear witness to Him that He is holy, imitating the Seraphim when they say “Holy” three times (Isa 6:3), repeating it without ceasing.

· To burn before Him sweet incense [4], imitating the living creatures and the heavenly elders who stand before the Lamb, each of whom has harps and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints (Rev 5:8)
· To offer the continual shewbread [4].
· To offer burnt offerings morning and evening [4].
· To observe weekly feasts (the sabbaths), monthly feasts (the new moons), and yearly feasts (the solemn feasts of the Lord our God), besides the Jubilee, etc. [4].

In his friendship with the king of Tyre he does not flatter, but bears witness to God: “for great is our God above all gods... the heaven of heavens cannot contain him [5-6]. Solomon feared that Hiram would think that the God of Israel is like his pagan gods, whom they confine in their temples.

entries.section: 2. He asks the king of Tyre for a skilled man

paragraphs.text: c. While taking pride in God in humility, he writes without shame: “Who am I then, that I should build him an house, save only to burn sacrifice before him?! [6]. Although he desires to build a great house, there is no basis of comparison between the greatness of the house and the greatness of the Lord Himself. He wanted to assure the king that God is not like the gods of the nations, dwelling in temples made with hands (Acts 17:24). Rather, he builds the house so that the priests and worshippers may find a place in which they express their love for God and their desire to worship Him.

d. What Solomon asks is that Huram supply him with a wise, experienced leader. For Solomon has skilled men in Jerusalem and Judah, whom his father David had previously appointed (1 Chr 22:15), and he needs a leader who can lead these skilled men.

The king of Tyre represented the Gentiles whom the people had not succeeded in driving out or enslaving, but he represents the few who could accept faith in God, and these were accepted as partners in this great work: erecting a house for the Lord.
Solomon's letter to Huram, king of Tyre, reveals the biblical view of the temple, or the house of the Lord.

First: The book, especially this letter, reveals that the main work of King Solomon is building the temple and organizing worship in it, and the whole nation's being occupied with meeting God through worship. It seems as though Solomon, with his wisdom and his activities, has nothing but this temple.

Second: The affirmation that God is not limited to any place, and that God declares His presence for the sake of His people, that they may enjoy meeting Him, and the expression of the mutual love between God and humanity, especially His people.

Third: Solomon's concern for the contribution of Huram and his men in building the temple is considered the way to reveal the calling of the Gentiles to the Gospel of Christ. This was a matter that God was preparing the Jews to accept throughout their whole history and through their prophets.

For Job was found, who was not of the seed of Abraham, and one of the books of the Holy Bible is recorded in his name. It was also said of him: “That man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil” (Job 1:1).
And the divine promise came to Abraham himself: “As for me, behold, my covenant is with thee, and thou shalt be a father of many nations” (Gen 17:4).

The Lord says: “Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted upon mine altar; for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people” (Isa 56:7).

v “No prophet is accepted in his own country” (Lk 4:24). Since Anathoth was the homeland of Jeremiah (Jer 11:21), it did not receive him well. Likewise Isaiah and the rest of the prophets were rejected by the children of their homeland, that is, the people of the circumcision... But we, who do not belong to the covenant but were strangers to the promise, received Moses and the prophets who proclaim Christ, we received them with all our hearts more than the Jews, who rejected Christ and did not accept the testimony to Him[1].
Origen

entries.section: 2. He asks the king of Tyre for a skilled man

paragraphs.text: Behold, I build an house to the name of the LORD my God, to dedicate it to him, and to burn before him sweet incense, and for the continual shewbread, and for the burnt offerings morning and evening, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts of the LORD our God.
This is an ordinance for ever to Israel. [4]

King Solomon explained the meaning of erecting the temple to Huram in a way that differs from what is stated in the Book of Kings, and Solomon brought out the concept of the house of the Lord: 1. The house of God in which He dwells in the midst of His people [3), that is, it represents the divine presence. 2. The personal house of God with every believer: “to the name of the LORD my God” [4]. 3. The house of holiness in which the fragrance of sweet incense rises [4]. When he says: “to dedicate it to him”, he invites us to imitate the Seraphim whom the prophet Isaiah saw, who says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple. Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly. And one cried to another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, LORD of hosts, his glory is the fulness of all the earth” (Isa 6:1-3). St. Cyril the Great has wonderful comments on this text touching our obligation to the holy life and the holy worship that befits being offered to the holy God.

v They fly, since they have nothing to weigh them down and bring them low. Their minds are always lifted up toward God; their authority is in the heights, they do not contemplate the things below, as we do, but keep their minds on the ineffable heavenly thoughts.

Their mouths offer praise; they confess in turn in order without weariness, as I see it, but in a manner that allows others to offer honors of praise in hymns of thanksgiving, since everything in the heights is carried out in exact order...
They say “Holy” three times, and conclude the hymn of praise with the Lord Sabaoth, thus pointing to the Holy Trinity of one divine nature.

In our confession we say that the Father exists, and so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. There is no difference in nature to distinguish between these, but one divinity perceived in three hypostases. This is confirmed to us by the holy Seraphim themselves, who say that the whole earth is full of His glory, having foretold in advance the future mystery of the Incarnation of Christ.

Before the Word became flesh, in truth Satan the avenger, the dragon, the apostate, ruled the earth under heaven, and creation was worshipped instead of the Creator who made it. But when the Word became flesh, all the earth was filled with His glory, and every knee bows to Him and every tribe and tongue confesses and serves Him, as the Holy Scripture says.
The blessed David offered that cry beforehand in the Spirit, saying: “All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord” (Ps 86:9; Phil 2:10-11)[2].

St. Cyril the Great 4. The house of the continual heavenly table, “for the continual shewbread”. 5. The house of perfect love, in which the believer offers all his life as a perfect burnt offering night and day. Solomon referred to the burnt offerings and did not refer to the sin offering or the trespass offering, for the book here does not speak of sins and their forgiveness, but transports us as if into heaven itself, where there is continual praise and burnt offerings of perfect love. 6. The house of continual joy, for celebrating the sabbaths, the new moons, and the solemn feasts of the LORD our God [4]. By the feasts of the Lord he means the great yearly feasts, which are the Passover, the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost), and the Feast of Tabernacles (Lev 23:4-44; Deut 16:1-17).

entries.section: 2. He asks the king of Tyre for a skilled man

paragraphs.text: And the house which I build is great: for great is our God above all gods. [5]

entries.section: 2. He asks the king of Tyre for a skilled man

paragraphs.text: But who is able to build him an house?
seeing the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain him? who am I then, that I should build him an house, save only to burn sacrifice before him? [6]
The Old Testament often spoke of the heaven of heavens (Deut 10:14; 1 Kgs 8:27; 2 Chr 6:18; Neh 9:6; Ps 68:33; Ps 148:4).
The Apostle Paul says of himself that he “was caught up to the third heaven” (2 Cor 12:2).

It is stated in the Targum: [For the lower heavens and the middle heavens and the highest heavens cannot contain Him, since He is the One who upholds all things with His arm by His authority. Heaven is the throne of His glory, and the earth the footstool of His feet, the deep and the whole world are supported by the Spirit of His word... So who am I that I should build Him a house?[3]]

The Jews believed in the existence of seven heavens, and the Old Testament speaks of “the heaven of heavens”, by which is often meant the third heaven, where the divine throne is and the dwelling of the saints with the heavenly ones in eternal life. Some, like Ambrosiaster, see that St. Paul was caught up twice, once to the third heaven, and again to Paradise, to which the right-hand thief went when the Lord Christ was crucified.

entries.section: 2. He asks the king of Tyre for a skilled man

paragraphs.text: Send me now therefore a man cunning to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass, and in iron, and in purple, and crimson, and blue, and that can skill to grave with the cunning men that are with me in Judah and in Jerusalem, whom David my father did provide. [7]
Archaeological remains and excavations have proved that the Israelites were not experts in the arts.

If God chose the children of Israel of old as a people for Himself, it was only to prepare the way so that the Savior of the world might come from the tribe of Judah, opening the gates of heaven to all nations and peoples. It is said in Isaiah: “And the sons of strangers shall build up thy walls, and their kings shall minister unto thee... Therefore thy gates shall be open continually; they shall not be shut day nor night; that the wealth of the Gentiles may be brought unto thee, and that their kings may be led” (Isa 60:10-11). And it is said in Zechariah: “And they that are far off shall come and build in the temple of the LORD, and ye shall know that the LORD of hosts hath sent me unto you” (Zech 6:15).

Solomon opens the gates of heaven to the peoples and nations, for the house that is built for God, whom the heavens and the heaven of heavens cannot contain, will it be limited to a particular people? It is the house of God, the Creator of heaven and earth, where He is pleased by the gathering of all peoples with Him and with His servants the heavenly orders.

entries.section: 3. He asks for the best kinds of wood

paragraphs.text: Send me also cedar trees, fir trees, and algum trees, out of Lebanon: for I know that thy servants can skill to cut timber in Lebanon;
and, behold, my servants shall be with thy servants, [8]

entries.section: 3. He asks for the best kinds of wood

paragraphs.text: And let them prepare me timber in abundance: for the house which I build is great and wonderful. [9]

Just as he asked him for a man who would be great in his skill and administration, so he also asked that the materials used to erect the house of the Lord be of the best kinds, “for the house which I build is great and wonderful” [9].

entries.section: 4. The pledge to provide for the workers

paragraphs.text: And, behold, I will give to the hewers that cut timber twenty thousand measures of wheat as food for thy servants, and twenty thousand measures of barley, and twenty thousand baths of wine, and twenty thousand baths of oil. [10]

King Solomon pledges that he will be very generous in providing for the workers. Solomon assured Huram that he does not offer the workers “bread and water” but enough and more than enough of wheat, barley, wine and oil. What concerns him is not only to give them good wages, but he also cares for their nourishment and comfort, since he offers them “wine”.
Barley, wine and ordinary oil used to be given as food to foreign workers[4].

entries.section: 5. The letter of the king of Tyre to him

paragraphs.text: 11 Then Huram the king of Tyre said in a writing which he sent to Solomon, Because the LORD hath loved his people, he hath made thee king over them. 12 Huram said moreover, Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, that made heaven and earth, who hath given to David the king a wise son, endued with knowledge and understanding, who builds an house for the LORD, and an house for his kingdom. 13 And now I have sent a cunning man, endued with understanding, Huram my father, 14 The son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre, skilful to work in gold, and in silver, in brass, in iron, in stone, and in timber, in purple, in blue, and in fine linen, and in crimson; also to grave any manner of graving, and to find out every device which shall be put to him, with thy cunning men, and with the cunning men of my lord David thy father. 15 Now therefore the wheat, and the barley, the oil, and the wine, which my lord hath spoken of, let him send unto his servants: 16 And we will cut wood out of Lebanon, as much as thou shalt need: and we will bring it to thee in flotes by sea to Joppa; and thou shalt carry it up to Jerusalem.
Then Huram the king of Tyre said in a writing which he sent to Solomon,
Because the LORD hath loved his people, he hath made thee king over them. [11]

Solomon's style, full of wisdom and dignity and honor toward the king of Tyre, had its effect on Huram, so he wrote to him congratulating the people of Israel on their wise king: “Because the LORD... hath loved his people, he hath made thee king over them” [11]. He did not say that because the Lord loves you He made you king, but “because the LORD hath loved his people”. Good leaders are a great gift that God gives to the holy people who are beloved of God.

Huram's answer to Solomon's letter reveals the spread of the knowledge of the Lord among the nations, and also suggests the response of the Gentiles to the Gospel of Christ and their delight in it. We may say that Huram here prepared the way, symbolically, for the Church of the Gentiles.
First: Huram, king of Tyre, played the role of Cornelius, the Gentile commander, and his household, whom he gathered in his house to meet Simon Peter, to listen to him, and to enjoy baptism.

Second: This work paves the way for what the Apostle Paul did in his concern for ministering to the people of the uncircumcision, or the Gentiles, and their response to his preaching. Huram's answer befits the Gentiles who thirst to know the Gospel truth and to believe in it[5].

entries.section: 5. The letter of the king of Tyre to him

paragraphs.text: Huram said moreover, Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, that made heaven and earth, who hath given to David the king a wise son, endued with knowledge and understanding, who builds an house for the LORD, and an house for his kingdom. [12]

Huram bore witness that the Lord loved His people, in that He made Solomon king over them, because he is the wise son of David, endued with knowledge, who builds a house for the Lord and a house for his kingdom. Is there not in this a prophecy, in the Gentiles' testimony to the true Solomon, the Lord of glory, the Son of David, who is the wisdom of God, who built the Church of the New Testament as an eternal house, the center of His heavenly kingdom?!

The king of Tyre looks on Solomon not only as a good gift from the Lord to His people, but also as a good gift to his father David: “who hath given to David the king a wise son, endued with knowledge and understanding” [12]. A wise and understanding son is a gift from God to his family.

It is clear from the style of King Huram that he had come to know the living God through his relationship with David as well as from the letter of his son Solomon, for he wrote: “Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, that made heaven and earth” [12].

The people of Israel walked in a spirit of godliness and uprightness, thanks to the godliness and conduct of David, which had its effect on neighboring peoples such as Tyre. Conversely, when the people worshipped the gods of the neighboring nations, at the same time these nations rose against them, defeated them and humiliated them. When man flatters evil, evil itself destroys him and takes away his dignity and his potential.

entries.section: 5. The letter of the king of Tyre to him

paragraphs.text: And now I have sent a cunning man, endued with understanding, (named) Huram my father [13]

Huram my father: in the original, Huram Abi. The word “father” here does not mean the father of the king; rather it is a title of honor for the chief or master of the workmen, who bears toward them a kind of fatherhood[6].

entries.section: 5. The letter of the king of Tyre to him

paragraphs.text: (The son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre)

skilful to work in gold, and in silver, in brass, in iron, in stone, and in timber, in purple, in blue, and in fine linen, and in crimson; also to grave any manner of graving, and to find out every device which shall be put to him, with thy cunning men, and with the cunning men of my lord David thy father. [14]

He sent to him a wise man in whose veins ran Israelite and Gentile blood, for his mother was of the daughters of Dan[7], and his father was a Tyrian. This wise man points to the Church of the New Testament, which includes members of Jewish origin alongside members of Gentile origin.

entries.section: 5. The letter of the king of Tyre to him

paragraphs.text: Now therefore the wheat, and the barley, the oil, and the wine, which my lord hath spoken of, let him send unto his servants: [15]

entries.section: 5. The letter of the king of Tyre to him

paragraphs.text: And we will cut wood out of Lebanon, as much as thou shalt need: and we will bring it to thee in flotes by sea to Joppa;
and thou shalt carry it up to Jerusalem. [16]

A treaty was concluded between the two kings: the king of Tyre provides Solomon with all his needs, and brings them to Joppa, and Solomon provides all the needs of the workers [15-16]. This treaty is mentioned in (1 Kgs 5:8-9).

entries.section: 6. The partnership of the foreigners in the work

paragraphs.text: 17 And Solomon numbered all the strangers that were in the land of Israel, after the numbering wherewith David his father had numbered them; and they were found an hundred and fifty thousand and three thousand and six hundred. 18 And he set threescore and ten thousand of them to be bearers of burdens, and fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred overseers to set the people a work.

And Solomon numbered all the strangers that were in the land of Israel, after the numbering wherewith David his father had numbered them; and they were found an hundred and fifty thousand and three thousand and six hundred. [17]
By the strangers he means the Canaanites who dwelt in the land of old and whom the children of Israel did not drive out.

entries.section: 6. The partnership of the foreigners in the work

paragraphs.text: And he set threescore and ten thousand of them to be bearers of burdens, and fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred overseers to set the people a work. [18]

Solomon employed the strangers, who had no right of inheritance in the Promised Land, as bearers of burdens and cutters of stone, and their number at that time was large, reaching one hundred and fifty-three thousand six hundred. He did not employ them for forced labor, but that they might earn their living generously, for the commandment came: [Thou shalt not oppress a stranger](*).

Besides the good things Canaan had because of its fertile land, the project of building the temple was huge, and many benefited from it. This was besides the building of the royal palace and other projects he undertook.
What do You want me to do, O Lord?
v You chose David the boy, the youngest of his brothers.
His father and his brothers despised him, but You do not despise the little ones.
You took this little shepherd, and set him on the throne to shepherd Your people.
Instead of the flute that gathers the sheep around him, You made him the sweet psalmist of Israel.
v You chose his son Solomon as a king wise in his youth.
You gave him wisdom from on high.
And with wisdom You gave him riches, glory and a good name.
You put it in his heart to build You a house, O You whom the heavens and the earth cannot contain.
v You gave him wisdom, grace and good management.
He made the king of Tyre a partner in building Your holy house.
And he called the strangers to work for You, O Holy One.
He found favor in the eyes of all.
And in his wisdom he did not exploit their love, but provided them with their needs in return for their work.
v O You who chose David and Solomon, and gave each of them the work according to his gifts and abilities.
What, then, O Lord, do You want me to do?
Open my eyes, that I may realize what my mission is.
Hold my hand and lead me, that my depths may be strengthened.
So that I may work not in slackness and faintheartedness,
but through You I can do all things.
Grant me not to turn to the right or to the left,
but by Your Holy Spirit to hold to the royal road!
Be my leader, my helper and my refuge, so that I never cease to work according to Your holy will.

entries.section: 1. The place and time of building the temple

paragraphs.text: 1 Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD at Jerusalem in mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared unto David his father, in the place that David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. 2 And he began to build in the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign.

In our commentary on the Book of Exodus, chapter 25, we saw that Father Methodius says: [The Jews prophesied about our condition, but we prophesy about the heavenly things; since the tabernacle (or the temple) is a symbol of the Church, and the Church is a symbol of the heavenly things[1].]

Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD at Jerusalem in mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared unto David his father, in the place that David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. [1]
This chapter is the only place in the Bible that declares that the site of the temple is Mount Moriah, on which Abraham offered his son Isaac as a burnt offering (Gen 22:2).

The temple was erected in the place where the first symbol, or practical sign, of the sacrifice of the Only-Begotten Son was fulfilled, which the Father offers for the salvation of humanity. This is the foundation and aim of the house of God: enjoying the sacrifice of redemption which the Lord Christ offered.

v Abraham, according to his faith, clung to the commandment of the Word of God, and with a ready mind offered a sacrifice to God, his only beloved son. For it pleased God to offer, on behalf of all his seed, His only beloved Son as a sacrifice for our redemption.
St. Irenaeus The choice of this place reveals God's view of His holy house in the midst of His people; it is the house of the Passover sacrifice that grants believers a joyful salvation.

Solomon did not need to study the site of the temple, for the site had already been determined for him beforehand (1 Chr 21:18; 22:1), to give him peace of mind, to save time, and to avoid long discussions among the leaders over choosing a suitable site for building it.
The site was fixed by a divine choice, and it was marked by the following:
a. It was in Jerusalem, because the Lord chose this city, and the Lord chose the place to put His name there. Also heaven has been called “Jerusalem which is above” (Gal 4:26).

b. On Mount Moriah, the mountain on which Abraham offered his son Isaac as a burnt offering (Gen 22:2). God gave Abraham a ram to offer in place of Isaac his son, and that was a type of the sacrifice of the Lord Christ. It was fitting that the house be built on the atoning sacrifice of Christ for the whole world.
c. In this place the Lord appeared to David and answered him with fire (1 Chr 21:18, 26), and there David offered an atoning sacrifice for the mistake he had committed.
d. David bought the place with his own money, and did not accept to offer the sacrifice on land given to him as a gift; he bought it through divine guidance.

e. The temple was erected on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, so that the Gentiles might realize that God is the God of all humanity, and not exclusively of the Jews apart from the rest of the nations.

f. In Jewish tradition there is a story about the choice of this site. It is said that two brothers lived in this area, one married and the other single. The married brother, out of love for his brother and feeling that his brother needed much expense to prepare for marriage, used every night to carry grain from his storehouses and go secretly to put it in his brother's storehouses. The single brother felt that his brother, being married and supporting a family, needed much expense, so he did the same thing every night. In the morning each of them would find that his storehouses had not diminished but increased, because of the blessing of the Lord upon him. One night the two met, each carrying some of his grain to put in his brother's storehouses. Each asked the other what he was doing. The two embraced, and in their joy at their love for one another they wept. In this place, where brotherly love was revealed, God chose that His holy house be built, the house of divine and brotherly love.

entries.section: 1. The place and time of building the temple

paragraphs.text: And he began to build in the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign. [2]

As for the time of beginning the work, it is said that he did not begin the work until the fourth year of Solomon's reign [2]. The three years were not spent in discussions, for the site was determined and the architectural plan prepared. Rather, this huge work needed many preparations. The number of workers was very large, and some may have needed to finish what was in their hands in order to devote themselves entirely to this work.

entries.section: 2. The dimensions of the temple and its adornment

paragraphs.text: 3 Now these are the things which Solomon founded for the building of the house of God. The length by cubits after the first measure was threescore cubits, and the breadth twenty cubits. 4 And the porch that was in the front of the house, the length of it was according to the breadth of the house, twenty cubits, and the height was an hundred and twenty: and he overlaid it within with pure gold. 5 And the greater house he cieled with fir tree, which he overlaid with fine gold, and set thereon palm trees and chains. 6 And he garnished the house with precious stones for beauty: and the gold was gold of Parvaim. 7 He overlaid also the house, the beams, the posts, and the walls thereof, and the doors thereof, with gold; and graved cherubims on the walls. 8 And he made the most holy house, the length whereof was according to the breadth of the house, twenty cubits, and the breadth thereof twenty cubits: and he overlaid it with fine gold, amounting to six hundred talents. 9 And the weight of the nails was fifty shekels of gold. And he overlaid the upper chambers with gold.
Now these are the things which Solomon founded for the building of the house of God:
The length (by cubits after the first measure) was threescore cubits, and the breadth twenty cubits. [3]

entries.section: 2. The dimensions of the temple and its adornment

paragraphs.text: And the porch that was in the front of the house, the length of it was according to the breadth of the house, twenty cubits, and the height was an hundred and twenty: and he overlaid it within with pure gold. [4]
The dimensions of the temple were handed over to Solomon by his father David, so there was no reason to change the dimensions.

It is noticed in the description of the temple that it is marked by a very great height in relation to its length and width: the length is like the width, twenty cubits, while its height is one hundred and twenty.
The height of the Holy Place was thirty cubits, while the porch that was before the Holy Place, and is not mentioned in the Book of Kings, was a separate, tall building in front of the Holy Place.

entries.section: 2. The dimensions of the temple and its adornment

paragraphs.text: And the greater house he cieled with fir tree, which he overlaid with fine gold, and set thereon palm trees and chains. [5]

As for the adornment of the temple, the woodwork was exceedingly splendid, and yet it was overlaid with pure gold [5]. The great house was covered with fir wood, which he overlaid with pure gold, and set upon it palm trees and chains.
Concerning the wood used in the house of the Lord, Origen sees it as wood that does not rot, pointing to knowledge or to chastity that does not age[2] or decay.

As for the gold, as we have repeated before in our commentary on the Holy Bible, it points to heaven, the palm trees point to victory, and the chains point to unity and the binding of all together as with golden chains. This is what marks the Church of Christ, as she bears the heavenly mind, and always enjoys a life of victory in her struggle against the devil and sin, and as all her members are united together as one body to the Head, Christ, and His holy heavenly Bride.
Origen sees that gold is the faith that makes the heart a heaven, and so it points to the heavenly things, as it points to the saints as being a heaven in whose hearts God dwells.

He says: [If you believe, you offer your heart and mind as gold!... For this reason Moses, who represents the spiritual law, declares “Take ye from among you” (Ex 35:5). If you can take these things from among you, then they are within you. You can offer the Lord something of your feelings, and of your words, etc.[3].]

And Father Methodius sees that gold points to the life of virginity, for he says: [He commanded gold (that vessels be made of it inside the Holy of Holies) for two reasons: first, that it does not rust, and second, that its color is to some extent close to the color of the sun. Thus it suits virginity, which bears nothing defiled or wrinkled, but always shines with the light of the Word. Through it we stand near to God, inside the Holy of Holies and before the veil, with hands undefiled like incense, we offer prayers to the Lord as a sweet and acceptable fragrance, in the (golden) censers of the twenty-four elders, which are the prayers of the saints[4].]

entries.section: 2. The dimensions of the temple and its adornment

paragraphs.text: And he garnished the house with precious stones for beauty:
and the gold was gold of Parvaim. [6]
The gold was the gold of Parvaim, one of the best kinds of gold.

entries.section: 2. The dimensions of the temple and its adornment

paragraphs.text: He overlaid also the house, the beams, the posts, and the walls thereof, and the doors thereof, with gold; and graved cherubims on the walls. [7]

entries.section: 2. The dimensions of the temple and its adornment

paragraphs.text: He graved cherubim on the walls; the Holy of Holies represents the heavenly throne of God by the presence of the two figures of the cherubim, and the veil is adorned with cherubim [14] who will not allow entry to the throne of God to any but those who bear the heavenly marks; even the walls are adorned with cherubim, because the house of the Lord is a second heaven!

entries.section: 2. The dimensions of the temple and its adornment

paragraphs.text: And he made the most holy house, the length whereof was according to the breadth of the house, twenty cubits, and the breadth thereof twenty cubits: and he overlaid it with fine gold, amounting to six hundred talents. [8]

entries.section: 2. The dimensions of the temple and its adornment

paragraphs.text: And the weight of the nails was fifty shekels of gold. And he overlaid the upper chambers with gold. [9]
The beams, the thresholds, the walls and the doors were overlaid with gold.

If the temple points to the heart of the believer, as the Apostle Paul says: “Ye are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwelleth in you” (1 Cor 3:16), and gold points to the heavenly things, then it befits the believer that all his inner life and conduct bear a heavenly mark.

Likewise the Holy of Holies, whose length is like its breadth, twenty cubits, is all overlaid with gold. Even the nails were of gold, and also its upper chambers, or its ceiling, were overlaid with gold.
The temple was adorned with precious stones as a symbol of heaven, since all its walls and gates and foundations are adorned with precious stones and pearls (Rev 21:18-21).

entries.section: 3. The two cherubim in the Holy of Holies

paragraphs.text: 10 And in the most holy house he made two cherubims of image work, and overlaid them with gold. 11 And the wings of the cherubims were twenty cubits long: one wing of the one cherub was five cubits, reaching to the wall of the house: and the other wing was likewise five cubits, reaching to the wing of the other cherub. 12 And one wing of the other cherub was five cubits, reaching to the wall of the house: and the other wing was five cubits also, joining to the wing of the other cherub. 13 The wings of these cherubims spread themselves forth twenty cubits: and they stood on their feet, and their faces were inward.
And in the most holy house he made two cherubims of image work, and overlaid them with gold. [10]
Since the word “cherub” means “knowledge”, Origen sees that the two cherubim are described as golden because they point to the abundance of (heavenly) knowledge[5].

entries.section: 3. The two cherubim in the Holy of Holies

paragraphs.text: And the wings of the cherubims were twenty cubits long: one wing of the one cherub was five cubits, reaching to the wall of the house: and the other wing was likewise five cubits, reaching to the wing of the other cherub. [11]

entries.section: 3. The two cherubim in the Holy of Holies

paragraphs.text: And one wing of the other cherub was five cubits, reaching to the wall of the house: and the other wing was five cubits also, joining to the wing of the other cherub. [12]

If the length of the wings of the two cherubim together is twenty cubits, five cubits for each wing, then the two wings are stretched out to occupy the whole width of the Holy of Holies, as though the Holy of Holies represents heaven and none is in it but one who bears the mark of heaven. It befits all people, when they meet the Lord, to enjoy the heavenly marks, and for dust to have no place in their hearts.

entries.section: 3. The two cherubim in the Holy of Holies

paragraphs.text: The wings of these cherubims spread themselves forth twenty cubits: and they stood on their feet, and their faces were inward. [13]

Before the building of the temple the two cherubim were on the cover of the ark of the covenant, and their size was relatively small. But after the temple was built, their size became large. Each wing extended five cubits.

The two cherubim stood, the wing of each touching the wing of the other, and the other wing touching the wall. So the extent of the four outspread wings reaches 20 cubits, that is, the width of the Holy of Holies [8, 12-13]. Their faces were turned inward toward the ark of the covenant. They appear as two servants of the invisible God, as though they invite all believers, Levitical priests and people, to join them in worshipping God, and not to worship them.

entries.section: 4. The veil of the temple

paragraphs.text: And he made the vail of blue, and purple, and crimson, and fine linen, and wrought cherubims thereon. [14]

The veil of the temple screens the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies. This veil reveals the need of humanity, even of those who worship God, for reconciliation with God, so that they may pass over into the heavenly things. This was fulfilled by the Cross of the Lord Christ, where the veil of the temple was rent, not by a human hand, but by the work of the Savior Himself.

The veil was made of different materials and various colors: blue, purple, crimson and fine linen [14]. The blue points to heaven; purple is worn by kings, crimson is the color of blood, and the white linen points to purity and cleanness. So it befits the believer to bear the heavenly mark, and to walk as a king with authority who does not fear the powers of darkness, enjoying the blood of the Lord Christ that forgives sins, and living in purity and chastity!
We have previously spoken of what each of the blue, the purple, the crimson and the linen symbolizes, in the commentary on Exodus chapter 25:

Origen sees that purple points to the radiance of love[6], and also points to fire[7]. The true Christian bears fire in his heart, the fire of the Holy Spirit, who lights up the way and burns the thorns that choke the soul.

Crimson points to the blood of the Lord Christ the Savior, for the crimson that we offer is our witness to Him unto blood, as the Apostle says: “For thy sake we are killed all the day long”; crimson pointed to martyrdom, whether by the shedding of the blood of believers in the ages of martyrdom, or by the life of daily mortification for the sake of the Lord.

The twined byssus (linen): since byssus points to the body, its being twined means being under control and restraint[8], as the Apostle says: “I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection” (1 Cor 9:27). Every struggle to control the body and master it in Christ Jesus is an offering to the house of the Lord.

entries.section: 5. The two pillars

paragraphs.text: Also he made before the house two pillars of thirty and five cubits high, and the chapiters that were on the top of them were five cubits. [15]

entries.section: 5. The two pillars

paragraphs.text: And he made chains, as in the oracle, and put them on the heads of the pillars; and made an hundred pomegranates, and put them on the chains. [16]

entries.section: 5. The two pillars

paragraphs.text: And he reared up the pillars before the temple, one on the right hand, and the other on the left; and called the name of that on the right hand Jachin, and the name of that on the left Boaz. [17]
Two pillars were set up before the temple, the height of each about 18 cubits (1 Kgs 7:15), and they were called Jachin and Boaz, meaning “the foundation, and the strength”.
Some see that these two pillars point to the house of David which the Lord established (2 Sam 7), and which continues by the power of the Lord.
There are chains on the heads of the two pillars that point to the unity of the whole nation, although it comprises the tribes.
If unity in the Old Testament was symbolized by chains binding the pillars, the Lord has given us His Body, so that all become different members in one body, having one Head, our Lord Jesus Christ.

entries.section: Warning

paragraphs.text: With the privileges that Solomon enjoyed, such as obtaining wisdom and building the house of the Lord and others, matters in which he appears to have surpassed his father, these privileges condemn him all the more if he does not make good use of them. St. Mar Jacob of Serugh says that when the wise Solomon was radiant, God sent down fire upon his offering, a sign of His acceptance of him and His pleasure in him, and when he sacrificed to the demons, He cast him from before His face. In his answer to the question: Why did the Lord, who knows all things, choose Judas as His disciple? And why did He create Satan, who resists the divine truth? he said:
v If you say, why did the One who knows all choose him, when He knew that he was deceitful and untruthful?
He chose him when he was beautiful, pure and clean, with no blemish, gentle and upright, and full of love for the Son of God.
And after He chose him, when he was fitting and full of beauty, he changed and lost his beauty and became hateful.
And if you say: If He knew that he would change, why was He pleased with his temporary, unstable beauty?
Much can be said against these things; if love is present, hear it with discernment.
If the Examiner of all had acted according to His knowledge, He would have nullified the plan of the creative power.
He would not have brought Adam, whom He created, into Paradise, nor have commanded him not to eat of the tree (Gen 2:17).
Nor would He have created Satan with the angels, nor made the cunning serpent that deceived (Gen 3:1).
And the upright course of the creative power would have been halted, and the world would not have come into existence as it has.
If He had acted according to His knowledge, He would not have formed the blasphemer in his mother's womb.
Nor would He have given the pagan to see the light, nor brought the unbeliever into the world at all.
The One who knows all brought Himself down, as it were, to unknowing, for the sake of His many mercies toward His creation.
He molded Adam, knowing that he would not obey Him, and despite His knowledge He did not wish to annul (his creation) as the Knower.
He brought him into the garden, knowing that he would not remain in it, and by His good will He brought him in so that he might stay there.
He commanded him much not to eat of the tree, and had He acted according to His knowledge He would not have commanded him.
So also, although He knew that Satan would fall, He created him with the host of the heavenly ones.
He made for the unbeliever a mouth and a tongue, knowing that he would disbelieve in Him, and He did not deprive him of them.
The Lord brought Adam into the garden so that he might remain in the garden; but as for his leaving it after he sinned, that goes back to him.
He commanded him to keep himself from the tree, and since he did not keep himself as he was commanded, this goes back to his own will.
He created Satan with the host of the house of Michael so that he might praise Him, but he envied and fell from his freedom.
When our Lord chose Judas, knowing that he would betray Him, he also resembled his father in his works.
While he was beautiful He called him to the good tidings with the beautiful, and after he became abominable He mixed him with those who crucified.
His Father also does not reject people as long as they are beautiful, for He sent down fire upon Solomon's offering (2 Chr 7:1).
When (Solomon) was beautiful, He answered him in prayer and gave him fire, and after he became a servant of the pagan sacrifices, He cast him from Him(*) (1 Kgs 11).
The Son of God also promised Judas a throne (Mt 19:28), and because he denied Him, He brought him down and gave him the gallows as his wage (Mt 27:5)[9].
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh
Raise up the wonderful temple of Your holiness within me!
v Allow me, O Heavenly One, to ask:
What were the feelings of the heavenly orders as they saw You become incarnate in the womb of the Virgin for my sake?
Are the heavens not pure before You, O Holy One?
Heaven and earth cannot contain You, O Unlimited One!
The heavenly ones are unable to comprehend Your surpassing mysteries!
How did You come down to our earth, You whom all the heavenly orders revere?
v You came down to us to raise from the earthly ones beings like the heavenly!
You raise us from the dunghill, and by Your Holy Spirit make us a temple for You!
v Solomon built You a temple on Mount Moriah, where Abraham offered his son Isaac to You as a burnt offering, in intention and love.
And David offered a sacrifice that You might forgive him, and rescue Your people from the plague!
And behold, You, the Lord of Solomon and his Savior, set up Your temple within me.
By Your Holy Spirit You turn my depths into a new Mount Moriah, and even make of my heart a wonderful Golgotha.
You declare the power of Your Cross and the joy of Your Resurrection within me!
v Solomon covered Your house with fir wood, with pure gold.
And behold, You clothe my heart with the incorruptible virginity, and turn my dust into a nature like the heavenly.
v Solomon garnished Your house with precious stones for beauty.
And behold, You adorn my soul by Your Holy Spirit, who grants me fellowship in the wonderful nature; by Your grace I become a living icon of You.
He takes of what is Yours and declares it to me.
He grants me love, joy, peace, chastity and goodness!
He shines in me with light, and dispels my darkness!
v It was not possible for any person to enter the Holy of Holies, except the high priest once a year.
Behold, You dwell in me, with Your heavenly Father and the Holy Spirit.
How great is Your love for humanity!
You raised her from her fall, and lifted her to surpassing glories.
You prepared her to enjoy sonship to You.
And behold, You prepare for her an inheritance that does not perish!
Grant that our hearts, minds, emotions and feelings become a chorus praising Your name without ceasing.
It shares the life of the heavenly orders.
What temple is this that is the work of Your hands?!

entries.section: 1. The brass altar

paragraphs.text: Moreover he made an altar of brass, twenty cubits the length thereof, and twenty cubits the breadth thereof, and ten cubits the height thereof. [1]

Whoever approaches the temple from the east finds the entrance to the court of the priests. At this entrance the people come with their sacrifices and their offerings that they bring to the Lord. On the right, on the south side, is the brass altar, where the fire is kept burning continually and the priests offer the sacrifices (Ex 27:1-8; 38:1-7).
The brass altar here is the counterpart of the Mosaic altar at Gibeon (2 Chr 1:6; Ex 38:30), but it is larger than it.

The things made of brass are the altar of burnt offerings [1], the molten sea and the lavers for holding water [2-6], the covering for the doors of the court of the priests [9], and some of the vessels of the altar and other things [10-18].
