The brass altar is not mentioned in the Book of Kings. Burnt offerings were offered upon it, and it was much larger than the altar that Moses made in the tabernacle of witness, whose dimensions were five cubits square, whereas the altar in Solomon’s temple measured twenty cubits square. For the people of Israel had increased, and had become numerous and rich, and it was hoped that they would be more godly through the experience of fellowship with God over these generations.

It was expected that the offerings for the altar of God would be far more abundant than before; therefore it was made of great capacity so that all the offerings could be placed upon it. For God had enlarged their borders, and it was fitting that they should enlarge His altars. What we offer ought to be in proportion to what is given to us.

The height of the altar was ten cubits so that the people worshipping in the outer court might be able to see the sacrifices of the burnt offering, and their hearts might be moved by it, and they might offer repentance for their sins, saying: It is of God’s mercy that I was not consumed, and this sacrifice has been accepted as an atonement for my transgression. Perhaps by this they would be led to the knowledge of the great sacrifice that would be offered in the fullness of time, the sacrifice of Christ! And perhaps their hearts would soar in the heavenly places when they saw the smoke of the sacrifices ascending.

The Holy Bible does not mention how they went up and carried the sacrifices to the altar. Some believe that they went up as upon a hill, without using steps (ladders), because the Law forbids this (Ex 20:26). Others hold that without doubt there was a sloping ramp for going up to the altar.

In the homilies of Origen on the Book of Joshua he gives us a living picture of the service of the altar and the sacrifices in the Old Testament as a type of what was fulfilled by the sacrifice of the Lord Christ on the Cross.

v We must explain the death of Moses, for if we understand how Moses died, we shall realize how Christ reigns. When you see the ruin of Jerusalem and the altar without sacrifice or offering or priests or Levites, when you see all this, say that Moses the servant of the Lord is dead.

And when you see that there is no one who comes three times (in the year) to appear before the face of the Lord, or to offer offerings in the temple, or to slay the Passover lamb, and eat unleavened bread, or to offer the firstfruits or to consecrate the firstborn child, then you realize the death of Moses the servant of the Lord.

But when you see the Gentiles entering the faith, and churches being built, and the altar being sanctified with the precious blood of Jesus Christ instead of the blood of sacrifices, and you realize that the priests and Levites are no longer occupied with the blood of goats and bulls, but with the word of God by the grace of the Holy Spirit, then it can be said that the Lord Christ has taken the leadership in succession to Moses...

When you see Christ our Passover sacrificed, and you eat the unleavened bread of sincerity, and the good ground of the Church bears fruit, thirty, sixty and a hundredfold, I mean the widows, the virgins and the martyrs. And when you see the people of the children of Israel increasing, that is, those who were born not of blood, nor of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God, and so became the sons of God, those who had been scattered and whom He gathered together into one in His person.

entries.section: 1. The brass altar

paragraphs.text: When you also see people keeping the Sabbath day, not by ceasing from work, but by putting away sin, when all these things come to pass, then you realize that Moses the servant of the Lord is dead, and that Christ the Son of God has all the leadership[2].”
Origen

entries.section: 2. The molten sea (the basin or laver)

paragraphs.text: 2 Also he made a molten sea of ten cubits from brim to brim, round in compass, and five cubits the height thereof; and a line of thirty cubits did compass it round about. 3 And under it was the similitude of oxen, which did compass it round about: ten in a cubit, compassing the sea round about. Two rows of oxen were cast, when it was cast. 4 It stood upon twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, and three looking toward the west, and three looking toward the south, and three looking toward the east: and the sea was set above upon them, and all their hinder parts were inward. 5 And the thickness of it was an handbreadth, and the brim of it like the work of the brim of a cup, with flowers of lilies; and it received and held three thousand baths. 6 He made also ten lavers, and put five on the right hand, and five on the left, to wash in them: such things as they offered for the burnt offering they washed in them; but the sea was for the priests to wash in.
Also he made a molten sea of ten cubits from brim to brim, round in compass, and five cubits the height thereof; and a line of thirty cubits did compass it round about. [2]

To the left of the entrance, toward the south side of the court of the priests, is the molten sea, in place of the small laver that stood in the court of the tabernacle of the congregation (Ex 30:17-21; 38:8).

This basin stands on the backs of 12 statues of oxen; perhaps these oxen point to the twelve tribes of Israel (2 Kgs 16:17), and they are in groups, each made up of three statues of oxen, each facing a different direction.
The priests were bound to keep their hands and feet clean, or else they were exposed to death (Ex 30:20).
The water for drinking in the Holy Bible points to the Holy Spirit (Jn 7:37-39), while the water for washing points to the word of God (Ps 119:9; Jn 15:3; Eph 5:25-27).

As the priests work in the temple they need water for washing, and need the word of God to wash their hearts by the Holy Spirit, the Giver of purity, holiness and continual renewal. This is what the Lord declared by washing the disciples’ feet before they partook of His holy Body and precious Blood on Holy Thursday.

This sea was like the laver in the Church of the New Testament, or like the baptismal font in the ancient churches. It is fitting for our consciences to be washed by true repentance, that we may serve the living God (Heb 9:14), and it is fitting for us to cleanse our hands and our hearts (Jas 4:8), so that we may hear the words of the Lord Christ: [He that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet], and be renewed by his repentance each time he enters to serve (Jn 13:10).

Josephus, the Jewish historian, holds that it was called a sea because of its enormous size. Others hold that it bore this name because of its symbolic work, for Solomon’s sea is a symbol of the first waters in creation, over which the Spirit of God was moving.
The altar and the sea are both symbols of their counterparts in the heavenly temple, made not with human hands.

paragraphs.text: The sea, or basin, was spacious. The rabbinic commentators believe that the priests used to bathe in it, immersing themselves in it [6].

entries.section: 2. The molten sea (the basin or laver)

paragraphs.text: He made also ten lavers, and put five on the right hand, and five on the left, to wash in them:
such things as they offered for the burnt offering they washed in them; but the sea was for the priests to wash in. [6]

There are ten bases of brass adorned with lions and oxen and cherubim, and upon each base a laver holding 230 gallons of water. These bases with their lavers are in the court of the priests on the right, and they stand on wheels that can easily be moved; they are used for washing the sacrifices, and perhaps for cleaning the temple in general.
When the water became dirty, it was poured out in a suitable place, and the lavers were filled with clean water from the molten sea.

These bases bearing the lavers are exceedingly beautiful with their many ornaments, so that the priests, the Levites and the people may realize that God sees in holiness and purity a special beauty, and that there is no separation between holiness and beauty (Ex 28:2; Ps 29:2; 69:6, 9; 110:3).

As for the laver, in the tabernacle of the congregation there was one laver, because all the priests were of the tribe of Levi, and even kings were not permitted to practice the priestly work. But in the temple, which points to the Church of the New Testament, there were ten lavers, five on the right and five on the left, because the priests of the New Testament are not bound to a particular tribe or a particular nation, for in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek; rather, all the priests are hidden in the greatest heavenly High Priest, our Lord Jesus Christ.
Such things as they offered for the burnt offering they washed in them [6]; for as the priests had to wash, so the sacrifices are washed. And we must cast away, with all diligence, all evil thoughts.

entries.section: 3. The golden candlesticks and the tables

paragraphs.text: 7 And he made ten candlesticks of gold according to their form, and set them in the temple, five on the right hand, and five on the left. 8 He made also ten tables, and placed them in the temple, five on the right side, and five on the left. And he made an hundred basons of gold.
And he made ten candlesticks of gold according to their form, and set them in the temple, five on the right hand, and five on the left. [7]
A spacious place to which the light of day does not reach needs these candlesticks.
Josephus exaggerated in saying that there were ten thousand lampstands in the temple.
It resembles the lampstand that was in the tabernacle of the congregation.
The word of God is a shining lamp that gives light in a dark world.

In the days of Moses there was one lampstand, namely the five books of Moses (the Torah). The addition of other lampstands here points to the addition of other holy books. Thus the light shines more brightly, and the lampstands, that is, the churches, multiply (Rev 1:20).

Moses established one lampstand, which is the Jewish church, but in the temple of the Gospel it was multiplied, not only because of the many believers from among the Jews, but the churches also multiplied from all the Gentiles and peoples.

entries.section: 3. The golden candlesticks and the tables

paragraphs.text: He made also ten tables, and placed them in the temple, five on the right side, and five on the left.
And he made an hundred basons of gold. [8]

In (1 Kgs 7:48) it mentions one table of the shewbread, because the aim of that book is to affirm the establishment of the kingdom of Israel, which was preparing the way for the coming of the Messiah, the Savior; but (2 Chr 4:8) points to ten tables in the temple, five on the right and five on the left, as though the Church of the New Testament, as a symbol of heaven, opens its doors to the new Israel in which the Jews are dissolved among the Gentiles, so that Christ offers Himself as heavenly bread to the peoples coming from the east and coming from the west, that is, from the ends of the world to its ends, without favoring any particular nation.
Perhaps twelve loaves were placed on each table, for as the house of the Lord grew greater, the service also grew greater. For in my Father’s house there is bread enough for the whole family.
These tables had a hundred basons or dishes of gold, for the table of the Lord is well prepared.

paragraphs.text: 11 And Huram made the pots, and the shovels, and the basons. And Huram finished the work that he was to make for king Solomon for the house of God; 12 To wit, the two pillars, and the pommels, and the chapiters which were on the top of the two pillars, and the two wreaths to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were on the top of the pillars; 13 And four hundred pomegranates on the two wreaths; two rows of pomegranates on each wreath, to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were upon the pillars. 14 He made also bases, and lavers made he upon the bases; 15 One sea, and twelve oxen under it. 16 The pots also, and the shovels, and the fleshhooks, and all their instruments, did Huram my father make to king Solomon for the house of the LORD of bright brass. 17 In the plain of Jordan did the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredathah. 18 Thus Solomon made all these vessels in great abundance: for the weight of the brass could not be found out. 19 And Solomon made all the vessels that were for the house of God, the golden altar also, and the tables whereon the shewbread was set; 20 Moreover the candlesticks with their lamps, that they should burn after the manner before the oracle, of pure gold; 21 And the flowers, and the lamps, and the tongs, made he of gold, and that perfect gold; 22 And the snuffers, and the basons, and the spoons, and the censers, of pure gold: and the entrance of the house, the inner doors thereof for the most holy place, and the doors of the house of the temple, were of gold.
And Huram made the pots, and the shovels, and the basons. And Huram finished the work that he was to make for king Solomon for the house of God: [11]

entries.section: 5. Holy vessels and other things

paragraphs.text: To wit, the two pillars, and the pommels, and the chapiters which were on the top of the two pillars, and the two wreaths, to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were on the top of the pillars [12]
Here we see a brief summary of the things made of brass.

The following is noticed here: 1. Huram was a skilled, careful and conscientious craftsman, for he accomplished everything that was asked of him [11]. The king of Tyre called him “Huram my father,” and Solomon also called him so, because he excelled in his work, and he was counted a father of all the skilled craftsmen. 2. Solomon was very generous, for he made very many vessels [18] of every kind, so that the work in the temple might be completed quickly, and so that there might be vessels to be used whenever vessels were damaged.

The contributions came generously, and he also gave generously. And when he had made enough vessels for that time, he could not use the brass that remained for his own purposes, because it was dedicated to God and must be used for His service alone.

paragraphs.text: And Solomon made all the vessels that were for the house of God, the golden altar also, and the tables whereon the shewbread was set [19]

The golden altar: it stands before the veil that separates the Holy of Holies from the Holy Place. Upon it the priests offer incense in the morning and evening, and they tend the golden lampstand (Ex 30:1-10; 37:25-29).
The offering up of incense points to the lifting up of prayers to God (Ps 141:1-2; Rev 5:8; Lk 1:8-10).
God gave Moses the special blend for the incense offered in the tabernacle of the congregation and the temple (Ex 30:34-38); no one may use this blend for any other purpose.

On the Day of Atonement the high priest uses the blood to cleanse and purify the golden altar (Ex 30:10). We cannot draw near to God without the atoning blood of the Lord Christ; for we may draw near only with clean hands and a pure heart (Ps 24:3-5).
Incense was burned upon it; perhaps it was made large, as was done with the brass altar.
Only here does the Holy Bible refer to a multitude of tables of the shewbread.

entries.section: 1. Bringing the holy things into the house

paragraphs.text: 1 Thus all the work that Solomon made for the house of the LORD was finished: and Solomon brought in all the things that David his father had dedicated; and the silver, and the gold, and all the instruments, put he among the treasures of the house of God.

Solomon was concerned to transfer the ark of the covenant from the city of David to the great house of the Lord that he had prepared, and he did not refer to the brass altar that Moses the prophet had set up in the wilderness; rather, a brass altar specific to the temple was set up.

The ark found its rest in the house of the Lord. The priests drew the staves out of the ark, so that the ends of the staves were seen from the ark, a sign that the journey of the wilderness had ended.

The ark of the covenant points to the Lord Christ, who dwelt among us by His Incarnation, that He might carry us over as to heaven, where our souls are settled and find rest in Him, while He is in us as His holy temple. By the saving work of Christ, He raised up from us a new earth and a new heaven in which His righteousness dwells in us.
Thus all the work that Solomon made for the house of the LORD was finished.
And Solomon brought in all the things that David his father had dedicated;
and the silver, and the gold, and all the instruments, put he among the treasures of the house of God. [1]
The book took every opportunity to point out that David had prepared all that was possible for the house of the Lord [1].

All the holy vessels, and also the silver and gold dedicated to the house, were placed in the treasuries of the temple, and there was no need for a celebration of bringing them into the treasuries, for it is the temple that sanctifies the gold, not the gold that sanctifies the temple (Mt 23:17).
Solomon took nothing of what his father had dedicated to the temple, or what the leaders or the people had given, or what had been placed in the palace treasuries for use in time of need.

entries.section: 2. Bringing up the ark of the covenant into the house

paragraphs.text: 2 Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel, and all the heads of the tribes, the chief of the fathers of the children of Israel, unto Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion. 3 Wherefore all the men of Israel assembled themselves unto the king in the feast which was in the seventh month. 4 And all the elders of Israel came; and the Levites took up the ark. 5 And they brought up the ark, and the tabernacle of the congregation, and all the holy vessels that were in the tabernacle, these did the priests and the Levites bring up. 6 Also king Solomon, and all the congregation of Israel that were assembled unto him before the ark, sacrificed sheep and oxen, which could not be told nor numbered for multitude. 7 And the priests brought in the ark of the covenant of the LORD unto his place, to the oracle of the house, into the most holy place, even under the wings of the cherubims: 8 For the cherubims spread forth their wings over the place of the ark, and the cherubims covered the ark and the staves thereof above. 9 And they drew out the staves of the ark, that the ends of the staves were seen from the ark before the oracle; but they were not seen without. And there it is unto this day. 10 There was nothing in the ark save the two tables which Moses put therein at Horeb, when the LORD made a covenant with the children of Israel, when they came out of Egypt.

Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel, and all the heads of the tribes, the chief of the fathers of the children of Israel, unto Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David (which is Zion). [2]

It was fitting that the ark of the covenant be brought in with great reverence. True, new vessels were made for the temple, of large sizes suited to the size of the temple and the size of the service, which had grown far beyond what it had been in the tabernacle of the congregation. But the ark of the covenant, the mercy seat and the two cherubim upon the mercy seat all remained as they were, because the presence of God and His grace do not change however much the size of the temple building (or the church) changes, however much the number of those gathered for worship increases, and whatever the state of the Church may be in its material means. The Lord Christ affirmed that if two or three are gathered in His name, He is in the midst of them, as though they were two thousand or three thousand.
The ark of the covenant was brought in in the presence of a great multitude of the elders of Israel, who undoubtedly attended with reverence and in splendid array [2-4].

entries.section: 2. Bringing up the ark of the covenant into the house

paragraphs.text: Wherefore all the men of Israel assembled themselves unto the king in the feast which was in the seventh month. [3]
This took place on the day of the feast with great joy, and they most probably counted this occasion a feast.

and the Levites took up the ark. [4]

paragraphs.text: And they brought up the ark, and the tabernacle of the congregation, and all the holy vessels that were in the tabernacle, these did the priests and the Levites bring up. [5]

They brought up with the ark also the tabernacle of the congregation with all the holy vessels that were in the tabernacle. These things were not set aside, because they had been sanctified to God; therefore they were neither changed nor beaten out to be used in making new vessels, and most probably some of them were not fit for use because of their smallness, so they were kept as a memorial.
Solomon brought up the holy vessels that David had prepared, together with the ark of the covenant and the tabernacle of the congregation, in a grand procession to the temple.
To prepare for this great procession Solomon gathered with the heads of the tribes and the heads of the fathers in the tent that David had prepared.

entries.section: 2. Bringing up the ark of the covenant into the house

paragraphs.text: And they drew out the staves of the ark, that the ends of the staves were seen from the ark before the oracle; but they were not seen without. And there it is unto this day. [9]
The staves were drawn out because the ark would not be moved afterward. Also, the drawing out of the staves points to rest, for our Lord Jesus rests in hearts that are open to Him as in His temple.
As we prepare a place for Him in our hearts, being His kingdom, He settles in them, and grants us also to settle in His heavenly Kingdom, which He prepares for us that we may settle in it.

The Lord longed for the ark of the covenant to settle in His holy temple, and the Apostle Paul says: “Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? (that is, to bring Christ down from above:) Or, Who shall descend into the deep? (that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead)” (Rom 10:6-7).

“And there it is unto this day” does not mean the day on which the book was written, but the day on which the copy was written that was the source from which the writer copied, and they remained until the day of the destruction of Jerusalem (Ps 137:7).

entries.section: 2. Bringing up the ark of the covenant into the house

“There was nothing in the ark save the two tables which Moses put therein at Horeb” [10]. Aaron’s rod and the pot of manna were no longer in it.

entries.section: 3. Offering the song of praise to God

paragraphs.text: 11 And it came to pass, when the priests were come out of the holy place: (for all the priests that were present were sanctified, and did not then wait by course: 12 Also the Levites which were the singers, all of them of Asaph, of Heman, of Jeduthun, with their sons and their brethren, being arrayed in white linen, having cymbals and psalteries and harps, stood at the east end of the altar, and with them an hundred and twenty priests sounding with trumpets:)
And it came to pass, when the priests were come out of the holy place:
(for all the priests that were present were sanctified, and did not then wait by course). [11]
The priests were sanctified when they came out of the Holy Place, for they had to come out so that the true King Himself might enter and proclaim His glory.
On that day not one course of the priests was present, but all the priests, for it was a general occasion that might not be repeated in the lifetime of the present generation of priests.
Sacrifices were offered, and it was fitting for all the priests to share in the celebration and to behold the glory of the Lord.

entries.section: 3. Offering the song of praise to God

paragraphs.text: Also the Levites which were the singers, all of them:

of Asaph, of Heman, of Jeduthun, with their sons and their brethren, being arrayed in white linen, having cymbals and psalteries and harps, stood at the east end of the altar, and with them an hundred and twenty priests sounding with trumpets. [12]
The Church of the New Testament inherited from the temple the worship of praise, in which there were choirs of praise. It was said that the number of harps reached more than 4000 harps.

The Church, the daughter of Zion, imitates David the king and prophet, “the sweet psalmist of Israel” (2 Sam 23:1), for she has found in the Psalms new, joyful depths in the light of the work of the Son of David on the Cross, His Resurrection and His Ascension into heaven. The Apostle Paul defined the Kingdom of God as joy in the Lord (Rom 14:17).
v Whatever you do, do it well; by this you praise God[1].

v If even the angels, whose nature is simple and spiritual, are said to have tongues with which they sing hymns to their God and Creator, and offer Him thanksgivings without ceasing, how much more is it fitting for the spiritual bodies of men to do this after the resurrection, for all the members of the glorified body will have tongues in their mouths, giving voice to their speaking tongues, and so they will utter divine hymns overflowing with words of their love and their joys that fill their feelings[2].
St. Augustine v Praising God is a work proper to the angels.

v The Psalms give the soul tranquility and grant it peace, and calm in it the confusion of thoughts and the accumulation of desires... This book is the book of love... it is a weapon against Satan... it is a cause of rest after the toil of the day... it is the consolation of the aged... it is the source of our holy joys and sorrows... it is a wonderful hymn, it is the voice of the Church, it is incense of sweet fragrance[3].
v Hymns sung quietly in the mind bring one into a state of joy and calm.

St. Basil the Great v Who has the power, however great his experience, to enumerate the causes that stir the heart so that it is kindled and set ablaze with fire, and that urge it to devout prayers of great zeal? But we will mention a few examples of them...
Sometimes the singing of a passage of the Psalms stirs in us a fervent prayer.
And sometimes the harmony of the melody in the voice of one of the brethren rouses sluggish minds to many supplications.
Likewise the manner of utterance, together with the reverence of the one who chants (the praise), kindles zeal in those who are with him[4].
Father Isaac

entries.section: 4. The cloud, and the glory of the Lord fills the house

paragraphs.text: 13 It came even to pass, as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD; and when they lifted up their voice with the trumpets and cymbals and instruments of musick, and praised the LORD, saying, For he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever: that then the house was filled with a cloud, even the house of the LORD; 14 So that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud: for the glory of the LORD had filled the house of God.

It came even to pass, as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD; and when they lifted up their voice with the trumpets and cymbals and instruments of musick, and praised the LORD, saying, For he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever: that then the house was filled with a cloud, even the house of the LORD. [13]
This event is not mentioned in the Book of Kings.

The priests were sanctified, and came out of the Holy of Holies; then a hundred and twenty priests sounded with trumpets amid the praise of the choir, and the glory of the Lord came down like a cloud.
The priests stood in amazement as the cloud prevailed over them, and they became as those in heaven, and were filled with the fear of the Lord together with surpassing love for God.

The Lord proclaimed His glory in the temple: 1. Not when the animal sacrifices were offered, but when the sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving to God was offered, in which God delights (Ps 69:31). 2. When 120 priests joined in the praise with the choirs of singers from the three Levitical families. And the priests with all their trumpets stood at the east end of the altar [12], which is the nearest place to the people. 3. His glory was proclaimed when they celebrated the eternal mercies of God and His goodness, for the phrase “for his mercy endureth for ever” is repeated 26 times in (Psalm 136). The glory of God is proclaimed by His mercy and goodness.

The cloud of glory filled the temple and gave it a divine beauty, more beautiful than the gold that covered it, or the precious stones that adorned it; yet this glory cannot be compared with the glory that was to be revealed by the good news of the Gospel (2 Cor 3:8-10).

By the cloud that came down and filled the house of the Lord, the Lord proclaimed His acceptance of this temple, and that it was like the tabernacle of the congregation that Moses made, for by a cloud He declared His divine presence when Moses entered the tabernacle (Ex 40:34).

v May he who has died with Christ and risen with Him offer praise. May he pray toward the east. For this too is written in the Second Book of Chronicles, that after the house of the Lord was finished by King Solomon, on the very feast of the dedication the priests and Levites and singers stood toward the east, giving thanks to God, and praising Him with cymbals and harps[5].
The Didascalia

entries.section: 4. The cloud, and the glory of the Lord fills the house

paragraphs.text: So that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud: for the glory of the LORD had filled the house of God. [14]

The priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud, for the glory of the Lord filled the house of the Lord [14], and this is evidence that the Levitical priesthood would cease from service when the Messiah came, in whom all the fullness of the Godhead would dwell bodily, and when He comes to His temple, for He is like a refiner’s fire, and who may abide the day of His coming, and who shall stand when He appeareth (Mal 3:1-2).

God declared His appreciation of the weakness and inability of the priests who stood to serve Him, as they could not bear the brightness of His glory. What happened to the priests here happened to the disciples on Mount Tabor when they entered into the cloud (Lk 9:34).

Josephus describes what happened, saying: [Now as soon as the priests had put everything in its place with regard to the ark and had come out, a thick cloud came down and stood there, and spread gently through the temple. It was a moderate, spreading cloud, not a stormy cloud such as we see when rain falls in winter. The cloud darkened the place, so that no priest could distinguish another. But it gave the thoughts of all a visible and glorious picture of God’s descent into this temple, and His joyful dwelling inside His tabernacle.]
O Lord, rest in my heart!
v In Your humility, You gave Your people the ark of Your covenant, a sign of Your presence in their midst!
In the wilderness, whenever the ark moved they moved, and wherever it stopped they stopped.
And when Solomon built Your holy temple, the ark was placed in the Holy of Holies.
There the staves were drawn out of the ark, for it had settled at last in the Holy of Holies.
It settled where Your people settled in the Promised Land!
v Let Your presence be revealed within me.
As the ark settled in the Holy of Holies, and as You rested in the house of Mary and Martha and Lazarus, rest in my heart, and let me rest in You.
v You declared Your acceptance of the house that Solomon built, in whose building the leaders and the people and even some strangers shared, by the coming down of the cloud of Your glory in it.
No priest could see his brother priest, for Your surpassing mysteries drew all their hearts and their eyes.
v Let my tongue praise You together with my heart.
And let my depths rejoice in You, and offer You a new song of praise!

entries.section: 1. The cities that Solomon built

paragraphs.text: 1 And it came to pass at the end of twenty years, wherein Solomon had built the house of the LORD, and his own house, 2 That the cities which Huram had restored to Solomon, Solomon built them, and caused the children of Israel to dwell there. 3 And Solomon went to Hamathzobah, and prevailed against it. 4 And he built Tadmor in the wilderness, and all the store cities, which he built in Hamath. 5 Also he built Bethhoron the upper, and Bethhoron the nether, fenced cities, with walls, gates, and bars; 6 And Baalath, and all the store cities that Solomon had, and all the chariot cities, and the cities of the horsemen, and all that Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, and in Lebanon, and throughout all the land of his dominion.

Some see that Solomon was occupied with practical construction, and although he was a man of knowledge, understanding, learning and wisdom, it is not recorded of him that he devoted himself to study and meditation. Yet his doing of many works shows that in his private life he cared for the word of God and meditated on it. This appeared through the work of the Holy Spirit of God, who inspired him with the holy books, namely Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs and Wisdom. Also his prayer in the temple reveals his study of the Law, especially the Book of Deuteronomy. All this suggests to us that he did not neglect his studies, his readings and his meditations.
And it came to pass at the end of twenty years, wherein Solomon had built the house of the LORD, and his own house [1]
That the cities which Huram had restored to Solomon, Solomon built them.

He cared for the church building, that is, the temple of the Lord and its annexes, as he cared for his palace and for building or renewing some cities, and for working for the comfort of his wife, the daughter of Pharaoh, outside the house of David, and for looking after the workers from among the Gentiles and the men of the Lord from among his own people, and for the ordering of worship and service.

Here we see Huram king of Tyre giving cities to Solomon, which points to God’s work with the Church of the New Testament, where the world hands over splendid cities to the Church of Christ, which receive the faith and are filled with peace.
He had already referred to these cities that the king of Tyre gave to Solomon (1 Kgs 9:11-13).

Here he did not mention the mistake that Solomon made in giving twenty cities of the land of Galilee to Hiram, which Hiram despised, calling them “the land of Cabul,” that is, trifling and worthless (1 Kgs 9:11-14). On the one hand, the king of Tyre despised these cities that were in the region of the Promised Land; on the other, there was unfaithfulness in this conduct, for Solomon disposed of the possession of the land of the Lord and handed it over to the Gentiles.

The Lord allowed him to build not only what the state needed, but also all that Solomon desired, and so he was extravagant in expenses and constructions. This afterward drove him to the luxury that corrupted his life, especially as he married many wives, for one reason or another, and he burdened the people with the payment of taxes, which caused the division of the kingdom immediately after his death, when his son Rehoboam took the throne. This is recorded in the Book of Kings, but Chronicles focused on the bright side connected with worship, and left the weaknesses and falls to be recorded by the Book of Kings.

entries.section: 2. The workmen whom Solomon employed

paragraphs.text: 7 As for all the people that were left of the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which were not of Israel, 8 But of their children, who were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel consumed not, them did Solomon make to pay tribute until this day. 9 But of the children of Israel did Solomon make no servants for his work; but they were men of war, and chief of his captains, and captains of his chariots and horsemen. 10 And these were the chief of king Solomon’s officers, even two hundred and fifty, that bare rule over the people.

As a king, a commander and a man of affairs, he did not seek his personal comfort, but employed many hands. He realized that it was in the people’s interest to encourage employment by every means, so that the state might not be afflicted with unemployment.
As for all the people that were left of the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which were not of Israel [7]

entries.section: 3. His care for his wife outside the city of David

paragraphs.text: And Solomon brought up the daughter of Pharaoh out of the city of David unto the house that he had built for her: for he said, My wife shall not dwell in the house of David king of Israel, because the places are holy, whereunto the ark of the LORD hath come. [11]

The bringing up of the daughter of Pharaoh from the city of David to the house that Solomon built for her is, in the view of the Book of Kings (1 Kgs 9:24), a kind of distinction shown to her; but in the view of Chronicles, which is concerned with worship and holiness, it was not fitting for her to remain in the city of David, even if she had accepted the faith, because of the presence of her maidservants from Egypt, who might be idolaters.

It tells us of Solomon’s relationship with the daughter of Pharaoh. This carried a symbolic meaning. The Pharaoh kings were accustomed to give the daughters of their handmaids, who had no right to the throne, to the kings of the nations; but to Solomon Pharaoh gave his daughter as a lawful wife. She had the right to sit on the throne of Egypt if she had no son to inherit the throne. So this marriage is a sign confirming that Solomon had a lawful right in the land of Egypt. This conduct points to the submission of many kings and great men to the Lord Christ by their acceptance of faith in Him.

Solomon built a palace for the queen, the daughter of Pharaoh, and brought her up with her retinue outside the city of David. He wanted the city of David to remain holy, and he feared that the daughter of Pharaoh and her retinue might do things unbefitting the holiness of the city.

It is probable that the queen was an outsider, and perhaps some idols from Egypt were with her or with her retinue. Although, sadly, Solomon himself was afterward enticed by his idolatrous wives to build idolatrous altars.

Despite his good relations with the Gentiles, Solomon refused to let the daughter of Pharaoh dwell where the ark of the covenant was, even if she had accepted faith in God, for fear that there would be in the palace maidservants of hers from Egypt who were unbelievers.

entries.section: 4. The ordering of the service of the temple

paragraphs.text: 12 Then Solomon offered burnt offerings unto the LORD on the altar of the LORD, which he had built before the porch, 13 Even after a certain rate every day, offering according to the commandment of Moses, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts, three times in the year, even in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles. 14 And he appointed, according to the order of David his father, the courses of the priests to their service, and the Levites to their charges, to praise and minister before the priests, as the duty of every day required: the porters also by their courses at every gate: for so had David the man of God commanded. 15 And they departed not from the commandment of the king unto the priests and Levites concerning any matter, or concerning the treasures. 16 Now all the work of Solomon was prepared unto the day of the foundation of the house of the LORD, and until it was finished. So the house of the LORD was perfected.
The religious and priestly services are mentioned in [12-16], especially the sacrifices of the burnt offering, which is not referred to in the Book of Kings.

The book does not refer to the details of the works that Solomon carried out, but is concerned to affirm that he arranged the daily, weekly, monthly and yearly service of the temple, especially the burnt offerings and the praise.
Then Solomon offered burnt offerings unto the LORD on the altar of the LORD, which he had built before the porch, [12]

entries.section: 4. The ordering of the service of the temple

paragraphs.text: Even after a certain rate every day, offering according to the commandment of Moses, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts, three times in the year, even in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles. [13]
Solomon’s role did not stop at building the temple and celebrating its dedication, but he continued to offer the holy sacrifices according to the Law of Moses [12-13].

Daily sacrifices were offered without ceasing, and weekly sacrifices on every Sabbath, which are double what is offered daily, and also additional monthly sacrifices at the new moons, and yearly sacrifices at the three great feasts.

Solomon’s heart, burning with longing for daily worship and for offering burnt offerings, incense and praises, was carrying this out according to the Law through the priests and Levites. In this period, before he turned aside after idolatrous women, he did not practice worship as a literal, routine work; rather, while keeping to good order according to the Law and the ordinance, he took part with his whole inner being, enjoying fellowship with God, offering prayers and enjoying heavenly thought through the shadows of the Old Testament.

He clung to God and loved Him, and felt with Jeremiah the prophet that the mercies of the Lord are new every morning (Lam 3:23). It is as though he repeated with him his saying: [The LORD is my portion, saith my soul; therefore will I hope in him] (Lam 3:24).
v What are burnt offerings? The sacrifice burned entirely with fire; when the animal is placed on the altar and burned with fire, it is called a burnt offering.
May the divine fires lift us up wholly, and may we be kindled entirely...
Not only our souls are lifted up by this fire of wisdom, but our body also, as it receives immortality. Let it then be offered as a burnt offering, and death will be swallowed up!

According to the number of his sons, as it is written, he rose up early in the morning and offered burnt offerings for each of them, cleansing them not only from unclean deeds but also from evil thoughts.

entries.section: 1. The queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon and her honoring of him

paragraphs.text: 1 And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon, she came to prove Solomon with hard questions at Jerusalem, with a very great company, and camels that bare spices, and gold in abundance, and precious stones: and when she was come to Solomon, she communed with him of all that was in her heart. 2 And Solomon told her all her questions: and there was nothing hid from Solomon which he told her not. 3 And when the queen of Sheba had seen the wisdom of Solomon, and the house that he had built, 4 And the meat of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their apparel; his cupbearers also, and their apparel; and his burnt offerings that he offered up in the house of the LORD; there was no more spirit in her. 5 And she said to the king, “It was a true report which I heard in mine own land of thine acts, and of thy wisdom: 6 Howbeit I believed not their words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it: and, behold, the one half of the greatness of thy wisdom was not told me: for thou exceedest the fame that I heard. 7 Happy are thy men, and happy are these thy servants, which stand continually before thee, and hear thy wisdom. 8 Blessed be the LORD thy God, which delighted in thee to set thee on his throne, to be king for the LORD thy God: because thy God loved Israel, to establish them for ever, therefore made he thee king over them, to do judgment and justice.” 9 And she gave the king an hundred and twenty talents of gold, and of spices great abundance, and precious stones: neither was there any such spice as the queen of Sheba gave king Solomon. 10 And the servants also of Huram, and the servants of Solomon, which brought gold from Ophir, brought algum trees and precious stones. 11 And the king made of the algum trees terraces to the house of the LORD, and to the king's palace, and harps and psalteries for singers: and there were none such seen before in the land of Judah. 12 And king Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all her desire, whatsoever she asked, beside that which she had brought unto the king. So she turned, and went away to her own land, she and her servants.

This story is told in detail in the First Book of Kings, and the Lord Christ Himself referred to it (Mt 12:42). The following is noticeable in this story: 1. The meeting of the queen of Sheba with Solomon is considered a call addressed to every person to meet One who is greater than Solomon, namely the Wisdom of God Himself, the Creator of Solomon and the One who gave him wisdom. The Lord Christ reproached the Jews who did not receive Him, while the queen of Sheba, who was of the Gentiles, came to Solomon to hear him.

entries.section: 1. The queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon and her honoring of him

paragraphs.text: What the queen of Sheba enjoyed in her meeting with Solomon cannot be compared with what we enjoy in our meeting and fellowship with the Lord of Solomon and his Savior. 2. Solomon did not invite the queen of Sheba to visit him, nor did she need to investigate the facts about Solomon, but she hurried to see with her own eyes [6]. His glory drew her.

The person of Solomon attracted many, even kings, and in this he differs from many kings who gained worldwide fame: on the one hand, he did not gain his fame by wars and violence, but by the spirit of wisdom together with peace. In his days as king, his kingdom extended for forty years, and we do not hear that he fought any battle with any of the nations or peoples. On the other hand, his relationship with the kings and peoples carried mutual respect, for he exchanged precious gifts with the queen of Sheba, and generously.

entries.section: 1. The queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon and her honoring of him

paragraphs.text: When she met him she realized that what she touched was far greater than what she had heard about him. So also when our Christ reveals His glory in us, His fragrant aroma in us bears witness for us, and we are ready to answer everyone who asks us a reason of the hope that is in us (1 Pet 3:15). 3. Hiram, king of Tyre, offered Solomon much gold and timber and other building materials, and also men skilled in building and workmen, but he did not go to Solomon to become a disciple of his wisdom. But the queen of Sheba came to him and listened to his wisdom. 4. The queen of Sheba met Solomon, and her soul rejoiced, a reference to the Lord Christ, the fountain of joy for everyone who meets Him. 5. She blessed those who stand before him continually, because they see his face and hear his wisdom. 6. She highlighted his authority over all the kings from the river to the land of the Philistines [26]. Truly, those who honor God, He honors (1 Sam 2:30). Solomon honored God greatly, whether by building the Temple, adorning it and dedicating it, or by praising Him and thanking Him, or by consecrating what God gave him of wisdom and riches for the sake of the Kingdom of God and the service of His people. 7. The queen of Sheba bore many troubles and great expense to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and yet she considered that, having heard his wisdom, she was rewarded with much. The wisdom of Solomon was a symbol of the Hypostasis of Wisdom, our Lord Jesus, who draws souls and brings them into the bosom of the Father. 8. Solomon knew how to kindle the gift that was given to him freely, and he offered it freely to others. If any gifts were offered to him, they did not occupy him; what occupied him was that all should enjoy the wisdom of God. 9. What caught the attention of the queen of Sheba was the good management of Solomon's household, of those who worked with him and of his servants. Some see that Solomon, in his speaking about wisdom or the management of the affairs of worship and so on, drew the heart of the queen of Sheba to the Lord Christ, the only sacrifice of atonement, who is able to complete salvation for all who come from among men. 10. The influence of Solomon by his wisdom in the Lord was not only on his servants who served him, but also on their sons, for they took pride in being called “the children of Solomon's servants” (Ezra 2:55; Neh 7:57). 11. The queen of Sheba presented a living example of sincere love, for she praised God for His work with the people of Israel through King Solomon [8].

And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon, she came to prove Solomon with hard questions at Jerusalem, with a very great company, and camels that bare spices, and gold in abundance, and precious stones: and when she was come to Solomon, she communed with him of all that was in her heart. [1]

The queen of Sheba heard of Solomon through the merchants who pass by Sheba with their ships. Here the queen of Sheba presents a living picture of the true believer from many aspects: 1. The queen did not stop at hearing about Solomon, but moved to meet him and to prove him, not in doubt of what she had heard, otherwise she would not have come bearing these precious gifts, but she came to enjoy meeting him. In this she is a symbol of the Magi who, when they saw the star, moved with their gifts toward Jerusalem to meet the One born King of the Jews and to worship Him.

In contrast to this, when King Herod gathered the chief priests and scribes of the people together (Mt 2:4) and asked them where Christ should be born, they offered him the prophecy, but did not move to meet the Christ who was born.
v They prepared gifts for the King that He might be honored by them, so that they might enter into His presence with offerings when they beheld Him.
When they took care to prepare the offerings, the Truth arose to teach them what they must do.
They opened their treasures and brought gold, because He is the great King, and they took myrrh, because He would become one slain.
Frankincense serves to honor Him, because He is also God: they brought spices and myrrh and gold to be offered to Him.
They carried the treasures of their fathers with joy, to offer their offerings to the great King...
They became preachers while walking on the way, proclaiming that the King has dawned upon the whole world...
Wherever they journeyed and wherever they halted, they told His story (saying): Our way is directed toward a mighty One born in Judea.
On their way His teaching shone forth, and at their appointed times their words were heard.
In every place where they halted they sowed the glad tidings, and when they departed they recounted the news of His birth.
Their preaching spread over the miles of the road, and in its stages those tidings were chanted[1].

St. Jacob of Serugh The queen told him all that was in her heart, and he told her all that she wanted to know [2]. This relationship represents the relationship of the soul with her Christ. On her part she reveals what is in her depths, and her Christ on His part tells her His divine secrets which she longs to know.
It is fitting for the believer to open his heart before his Savior, and to enter with Him into an open dialogue.

The report of her visit to him reveals to us not only the greatness of Solomon's palace, but also the life that went on in the palace, from the food of his table and the sitting of his servants to the conduct of his ministers, even their apparel.
Most likely, as a Gentile, she was not taken to the house of the Lord, but she also knew of the burnt offerings which he offered through the priests.
The queen could not record her feelings about his life in his palace and his love and giving for the house of the Lord, but it was said: “There was no more spirit in her.”
What she saw and heard and touched was only a shadow, as happened with the Apostle Paul, who heard unspeakable words (2 Cor 12:4).

The queen realized that Solomon, his household and those who worked with him were the happiest people she had seen on the face of the earth! Here we recall what St. John Chrysostom wrote, that the Christian is the happiest person on earth.

entries.section: 2. The greatness of Solomon's court and his wealth

paragraphs.text: 13 Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred and threescore and six talents of gold; 14 Beside that which chapmen and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon. 15 And king Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold: six hundred shekels of beaten gold went to one target. 16 And three hundred shields made he of beaten gold: three hundred shekels of gold went to one shield. And the king put them in the house of the forest of Lebanon. 17 Moreover the king made a great throne of ivory, and overlaid it with pure gold. 18 And there were six steps to the throne, with a footstool of gold, which were fastened to the throne, and stays on each side of the sitting place, and two lions standing by the stays: 19 And twelve lions stood there on the one side and on the other upon the six steps. There was not the like made in any kingdom. 20 And all the drinking vessels of king Solomon were of gold, and all the vessels of the house of the forest of Lebanon were of pure gold: none were of silver; it was not any thing accounted of in the days of Solomon. 21 For the king's ships went to Tarshish with the servants of Huram: every three years once came the ships of Tarshish bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks. 22 And king Solomon passed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom. 23 And all the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon, to hear his wisdom, that God had put in his heart. 24 And they brought every man his present, vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and raiment, harness, and spices, horses, and mules, a rate year by year. 25 And Solomon had four thousand stalls for horses and chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen; whom he bestowed in the chariot cities, and with the king at Jerusalem. 26 And he reigned over all the kings from the river even unto the land of the Philistines, and to the border of Egypt. 27 And the king made silver in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar trees made he as the sycomore trees that are in the low plains in abundance. 28 And they brought unto Solomon horses out of Egypt, and out of all lands.

Since God, who is all-rich in wealth, glory, power and wisdom, was with Solomon, He poured out of what is His upon His beloved. History does not mention a king with the wealth and glory of Solomon, together with his wisdom and his ability to create an atmosphere of peace with the nations and peoples of his age. Yet the Lord Christ says that the lilies of the field, which appear for a day and wither, are more splendidly arrayed than Solomon was in all his glory (Mt 6:29).

Moreover, this book did not record Solomon's deviations and his fall, which are recorded in First Kings. Perhaps the Scripture offers us an important lesson, that even if the great and the wise may fall, and their fall is serious, it is not for us to expose them at every time. On the other hand, perhaps Solomon offered repentance for them, and therefore the book is silent about them, because they were forgiven him (Ezek 33:16). God in His love for man no longer remembers our sins as long as we have returned to Him and left the way of evil.
Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred and threescore and six talents of gold [13]

This weight of gold is equivalent to about 25 tons of gold. Yet the wise man later records for us his experience in the Book of Ecclesiastes: “Vanity of vanities; all is vanity.” And it is written in the Book of Proverbs: “Better is little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble therewith. Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith” (Prov 15:16-17).
Most likely she heard from him such words of wisdom while she saw the riches of his palace and the treasures of his storehouses, and so it was said of her: “There was no more spirit in her” [4].

God promised Solomon that He would give him riches and honor along with wisdom (2 Chr 1:11-12; 1 Kgs 3:12-13). Riches in themselves are not a sin, for Abraham was very rich, and gave all his wealth to his son Isaac (Gen 24:34-36). The management of wealth is not a sin; rather the love of money is a sin (1 Tim 6:7-10). Solomon himself wrote: “He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity” (Eccl 5:10).

v Do you want to be a virgin?... If you long for all this, overcome the flesh, defeat the lusts of the flesh, overcome the world in the Spirit of God, triumph over the vain temporal things which pass and grow old and corrupt and come to an end, overcome the dragon (Rev 12:7), overcome the lion (1 Pet 5:8), overcome the serpent (2 Cor 11:3), overcome Satan, by Jesus who strengthens you, by your hearing His words and your enjoying the Eucharist in God. Take up His cross and follow Him (Mt 26:24), He who purifies you, Jesus Christ your Lord[10].
St. Clement of Rome v After your victories, which flow from His victories, the angels also receive you and glorify you and serve you as guardians for you in everything[11].

v He was born in a manger, to raise you to the altar; He came to earth, to raise you to heaven; He found no place for Himself except in the manger of the oxen, that He might offer you mansions in heaven (Jn 14:2), and as the Apostle says: “Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich” (2 Cor 9:8). St. Ambrose v He feeds those who are counted among men as heavenly, until they reach eternity, setting aside the lusts of the flesh so that they fall shattered[12].
St. Clement of Alexandria

Origen v He who truly believes is wholly united with Him in whom are truth, divinity, essence, life and wisdom, and sees in Him all these, which are not in him who does not believe. For Christ is “the power of God, and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor 24:1); he who thinks that he sees the One God without power, without truth, without wisdom, without life and without true light, either sees nothing at all, or certainly sees what is evil[14].
St. Gregory of Nyssa
